question: After King Arthur broke his first sword in a duel against King Pellinore, the wizard Merlin took him to a remote misty lake hidden among the hills. A pale arm clothed in white samite rose silently from the still water, holding a long sword aloft. The Lady of the Lake — a sorceress who lived beneath the waves — rowed out to meet them in a small barge and asked Arthur to name her a gift in return for the sword. What gift did she ask for later in payment?
answer: The head of any knight or maiden she chose
choices: The head of any knight or maiden she chose
A measure of gold equal to the sword's weight
Three years of service at her lake
The first child born to Arthur and Guinevere
context: Excalibur was distinct from the sword Arthur drew from the stone. The Lady of the Lake later returned to claim her boon at Camelot and demanded the head of Sir Balin, who killed her instead — beginning a long chain of doom in the Round Table cycle.

question: Merlin once told the young King Arthur that the scabbard of his enchanted sword Excalibur was actually more valuable than the blade itself. The wizard pressed Arthur never to lose it — for as long as the scabbard hung at his side, the king could shed not a single drop of blood no matter how grievously he was wounded. Arthur did not believe him at first. What protection did the scabbard give its wearer?
answer: The wearer would not bleed from any wound
choices: The wearer would not bleed from any wound
The wearer's blade would never break or chip
The wearer would always strike his enemy first
The wearer could heal others by his touch
context: Morgan le Fay, Arthur's enchantress half-sister, eventually stole the scabbard and threw it into a deep lake. Without it, Arthur's later wounds bled freely — including the mortal wound he took at Camlann.

question: A young French knight rode into King Arthur's court at Camelot wearing armor stained from many roads. He had been raised by the Lady of the Lake after his father King Ban died, and she had taught him swordplay until he was the finest fighter in the world. He knelt before Arthur and asked to join the Round Table. His name became the most celebrated in Arthur's court — and the most tragic, for he would love the queen. What was this knight called?
answer: Sir Lancelot du Lac
choices: Sir Lancelot du Lac
Sir Tristan of Lyonesse
Sir Bors de Ganis
Sir Lamorak de Galis
context: Lancelot du Lac means 'Lancelot of the Lake', a reference to his foster-mother. In Malory's *Le Morte d'Arthur* he is the perfect knight in every way except his love for Guinevere — the flaw that brings down the Round Table.

question: On Christmas Day at Camelot, a giant knight rode into the great hall on a green horse, holding a holly bough in one hand and an enormous axe in the other. His skin and hair were also green. He challenged any knight to strike one blow at his neck with the axe — on the condition that he could return the blow exactly one year later. King Arthur's nephew Sir Gawain accepted. What happened the moment Gawain struck the green knight's neck?
answer: The knight picked up his own severed head and rode away
choices: The knight picked up his own severed head and rode away
The blow bounced off harmlessly as if striking stone
The knight transformed into a roaring fire dragon
The hall fell into a deep enchanted sleep for a year
context: The 14th-century poem *Sir Gawain and the Green Knight* is one of the great works of Middle English. The severed head spoke before being lifted, naming the Green Chapel where Gawain must come a year hence to receive his blow.

question: A year and a day after Christmas at Camelot, Sir Gawain rode through deep snow to the Green Chapel as he had sworn, to receive the axe blow that the Green Knight owed him in return. He had spent three nights at a nearby castle whose lord hunted each day. Each night the lord's wife offered Gawain a love-token; on the third night he kept a green silk girdle she said would protect him from death. When the Green Knight finally swung the axe, what did he do?
answer: Nicked Gawain's neck only and revealed himself as the castle's lord
choices: Nicked Gawain's neck only and revealed himself as the castle's lord
Missed wide and split a great boulder behind Gawain's shoulder
Vanished in a green mist as Gawain prayed under his hood
Sheared his head off cleanly with a single mighty stroke
context: The Green Knight was Bertilak, the lord of the castle, in enchanted form. Morgan le Fay had sent him to test Camelot's chivalry. Gawain wore the green girdle ever after as a mark of shame for hiding it from his host, and the Round Table all adopted green sashes in his honor.

question: Sir Tristan was sent by his uncle, King Mark of Cornwall, to escort the Irish princess Iseult home across the sea to be Mark's bride. Iseult's mother had given a maid a magical potion to be served to Iseult and King Mark on their wedding night, to bind them in love forever. By accident the wrong cup was filled. What happened when Tristan and Iseult drank from it on the voyage?
answer: They fell helplessly in love and could never love anyone else
choices: They fell helplessly in love and could never love anyone else
They were transformed into a pair of swans together
Their ship sank as the sea-god punished the broken oath
They became invisible to all but each other for one year
context: Iseult still married King Mark, but she and Tristan continued their affair in secret. The story was retold by Béroul and Thomas of Britain in the 12th century, and was the model for the Lancelot–Guinevere romance. Wagner's opera *Tristan und Isolde* (1865) made the love-potion scene iconic in Western music.

question: The young knight Percival, raised in the forest by his mother who hoped to keep him from chivalry's dangers, came one evening to a strange castle where a wounded king lay on a couch beside the fire. The king's wound — in the thigh — would not heal, and his country had become a wasteland. At dinner a solemn procession passed through the hall: a youth carrying a bleeding lance, then a maiden carrying a glowing covered chalice. Percival, taught not to question his elders, said nothing. What was the king called?
answer: The Fisher King
choices: The Fisher King
King Pellam the Maimed
King Lot of Orkney
King Bran the Blessed
context: In Chrétien de Troyes' unfinished *Perceval* (c. 1180), Percival's failure to ask the right question — 'Whom does the Grail serve?' — let the wasteland persist and the king continue to suffer. Asking would have healed both. Percival returned years later to ask the question and was named guardian of the Grail.

question: On a Pentecost morning at Camelot, a great red marble stone with a sword fixed in it floated down the river past the castle. Letters carved on the blade declared that none might draw it but the world's best knight. Lancelot tried and was rebuked by his peers; Gawain tried and was warned the attempt would cost him dearly. That afternoon a young knight in white armor rode in with an old hermit who declared him the Round Table's destined Grail-knight. What did this young knight do with the floating sword?
answer: He drew it easily and belted it on for the quest
choices: He drew it easily and belted it on for the quest
He shattered it across his knee in fury
He blessed it and let it sink back into the river
He gave it to his father Lancelot as an inheritance
context: Sir Galahad was Lancelot's son by Elaine of Corbenic. He was conceived through an enchantment that made Elaine appear to Lancelot as Guinevere. Galahad was raised in a convent and brought to Camelot to begin the Grail quest. He would later sit unharmed in the Siege Perilous, the empty seat reserved for him.

question: When King Arthur married Princess Guinevere, her father King Leodegrance of Cameliard sent a great wedding gift to Camelot — an enormous circular table built by Merlin years before, with seats for one hundred and fifty knights. One seat in the table was bordered in gold and inscribed with a warning. Any knight who sat in it who was not the destined Grail-winner would be swallowed by the earth or burst into flame. What was this seat called?
answer: The Siege Perilous
choices: The Siege Perilous
The Throne of Heaven
The Hermit's Chair
The Seat of the Cross
context: The Round Table's shape ensured no knight sat above another — all were equal in honor. Sir Galahad was the only knight ever to sit safely in the Siege Perilous when he arrived at Camelot for the Grail quest. After his death the seat was left forever empty in his memory.

question: After King Uther Pendragon of Britain died without an obvious heir, the bishops and barons could not agree who should rule. On New Year's morning a great square stone of marble appeared in the churchyard of London, with a steel anvil sitting on top of it and a beautiful sword driven through both anvil and stone to the hilt. Letters of gold ran around the sword. What did the letters say?
answer: Whoso pulleth out this sword is rightwise born King of all England
choices: Whoso pulleth out this sword is rightwise born King of all England
The hand that draws this blade alone shall bear my crown
He who freeth this sword shall freeth Britain from her chains
Let none touch this blade who cannot also touch the stars
context: Many great lords tried for years and failed. The fifteen-year-old Arthur drew it casually one afternoon when his foster-brother Sir Kay needed a sword for a tournament. Sir Ector then knelt and revealed Arthur's true parentage. Malory used Sir Thomas Malory's wording from *Le Morte d'Arthur* (1485).

question: The British king Aurelius Ambrosius (Arthur's uncle) wanted to build a great memorial at Salisbury Plain for the British nobles who had been treacherously killed by the Saxon leader Hengist at the 'Night of the Long Knives' feast. He asked the wizard Merlin how to make a monument equal to the slaughter. Merlin said only one set of stones in Britain would be worthy. Where did Merlin claim the giant stones originally came from?
answer: Ireland — they were the Giants' Ring on Mount Killaraus
choices: Ireland — they were the Giants' Ring on Mount Killaraus
Norway — they were the dragon-fang stones of Olaf
Italy — they were Roman ruins from a temple of Janus
Wales — they were the hill-stones the druids worshipped
context: In Geoffrey of Monmouth's *History of the Kings of Britain* (c. 1136), Merlin used his magical arts to move the stones from Ireland across the sea to Salisbury Plain. Modern geology has actually confirmed that the smaller bluestones of Stonehenge came from the Preseli Hills in Wales — a 250-km journey.

question: Years after Tristan had to leave Cornwall to flee King Mark, he married another woman named Iseult of the White Hands in Brittany, but could not love her in his heart. Wounded by a poisoned spear in battle, Tristan sent for the original Iseult of Ireland — the only healer who could save him. He told his wife: if Iseult of Ireland arrived, the ship should fly a white sail; if she refused to come, a black sail. The ship returned with the white sail flying. What did Iseult of the White Hands tell the dying Tristan?
answer: That the sail was black
choices: That the sail was black
That the ship had sunk in a storm
That his lover had married another
That the ship had been turned back by pirates
context: Tristan died of grief on hearing the lie. When Iseult of Ireland landed and found him dead, she lay down beside him and died of sorrow as well. King Mark planted a rose bush over Tristan's grave and a vine over Iseult's — they grew together and intertwined no matter how often Mark cut them apart.

question: King Arthur called all the surviving knights to Camelot at Pentecost each year and made them renew the oath that bound them to the Round Table. Knights who would not swear it were sent home. The oath required them to defend the weak, never use force against women, never give battle in a wrongful quarrel, and to grant mercy to any enemy who asked. In Malory's account, when did Arthur first establish this oath?
answer: After the great wedding feast where the Round Table arrived as Guinevere's dowry
choices: After the great wedding feast where the Round Table arrived as Guinevere's dowry
After the dragon battle when Arthur won the sword Excalibur
After the coronation when he drew the sword from the stone
After Sir Lancelot first arrived at the court from France
context: Malory's wording: knights swore 'to flee treason; by no means to be cruel; to give mercy unto him that asketh mercy; always to do ladies, damosels, and gentlewomen succor; and never to enforce them; and to fight in no wrongful quarrel for no law nor for no world's goods.' The chivalric code reached its full literary form in this scene.

question: In one of the loveliest of all Arthurian tales, King Arthur was captured by an enchanter and forced to ride alone seeking the answer to a riddle: 'What do women most desire?' He found the answer only when he met a hideous old woman in the forest who knew it — but she demanded as her price that the king's nephew Sir Gawain marry her. Gawain agreed without complaint for Arthur's sake. What was the answer the old woman gave?
answer: Sovereignty over their own lives
choices: Sovereignty over their own lives
Children who would grow strong and faithful
A husband who would die before they did
Beauty that would never fade with age
context: On the wedding night the old hag became a beautiful young woman named Lady Ragnell — she had been enchanted by a wicked stepmother. She offered Gawain a choice: lovely by day and hideous by night, or hideous by day and lovely by night. He told her to choose for herself. Her own choice broke the spell entirely. The tale survives in *The Wedding of Sir Gawain and Dame Ragnell* (15th c.).

question: Long before the affair was discovered, Sir Lancelot once rescued Queen Guinevere from the wicked knight Meleagant, who had abducted her into the cursed kingdom of Gorre. To follow her trail Lancelot lost his horse, and only one humiliating transport could carry him fast enough to catch up. In the 12th-century romance by Chrétien de Troyes, what did Lancelot ride?
answer: A cart used by criminals being driven to the gallows
choices: A cart used by criminals being driven to the gallows
A donkey too small to bear his weight
A blind ploughorse owned by a peasant
A wooden raft pulled across the river by a fisherman
context: Chrétien's poem is called *Le Chevalier de la Charrette* — the Knight of the Cart — exactly because of this humiliation. To ride such a cart was the deepest possible shame for a knight, equivalent to public branding. Lancelot's willingness to climb in proved his love for the queen overrode all worldly honor.

question: The Sheriff of Nottingham announced a great archery contest in the town square with a golden arrow as the prize, secretly hoping that the famous outlaw Robin Hood would not be able to resist the challenge and would walk straight into a trap. Robin came in disguise as a tattered beggar with one eye covered by a black patch. Each shooter had to plant his arrow in a clout target at the far end of the field. The previous best arrow was placed perfectly in the bullseye. What did Robin's shot do?
answer: Split the previous best arrow down the middle
choices: Split the previous best arrow down the middle
Knocked the target clean off its standing pole
Pierced the wand the target was hung on
Bounced from the clout and stuck in the king's chair
context: Robin walked up to receive the golden arrow from the Sheriff's own hand, untouched. He sent the Sheriff a letter that night with an arrow shaft attached, signed: 'Now you know who shot the golden arrow.' The trick has been retold in nearly every Robin Hood film since.

question: Robin Hood was crossing a narrow log bridge over a stream in Sherwood Forest when an enormous stranger met him coming the other way. Neither would step aside. Robin set down his longbow and quarterstaff, and the giant cut himself a tree-branch staff of equal length. They fought on the slippery log for nearly an hour. What happened to Robin?
answer: He was knocked into the stream by a single blow to the ribs
choices: He was knocked into the stream by a single blow to the ribs
He broke the giant's staff with one upward sweep
He surrendered when his quarterstaff finally splintered
He pulled the giant down into the stream with him
context: The giant's true name was John Little, but Robin Hood renamed him Little John for the joke. Little John was over seven feet tall in the ballads and became Robin's lieutenant and closest friend. The bridge meeting is the most-retold of all Robin Hood stories, from the 15th-century ballad *Robin Hood and Little John* onward.

question: Robin Hood once heard rumors of a fat fighting friar living in a hermitage by the River Skell, who wore a sword under his cassock and shot arrows as well as any Sherwood man. Robin sought him out to test him. The friar agreed to carry Robin across the river on his back — then dropped him in mid-stream. They fought neck-deep in water. When Robin tired, he winded his hunting horn for help. What did the friar do then?
answer: Whistled up his pack of fierce hounds against Robin
choices: Whistled up his pack of fierce hounds against Robin
Slipped under the water and swam to the far bank
Threw his sword aside and laughed in surrender
Cried out for the Virgin Mary to save him
context: Robin and the friar wrestled and battled until both fell into the river exhausted. Then they laughed, sat on the bank, and Robin asked Friar Tuck to join the band. Tuck became Sherwood's chaplain and chief drinker. The story is in the ballad *Robin Hood and the Curtal Friar*.

question: Returning from the Third Crusade and a long captivity in Austria, King Richard the Lionheart of England disguised himself as a black-robed abbot to ride through Sherwood Forest and see for himself whether the rumors of the famous outlaw Robin Hood were true. Robin's men ambushed the king's party and brought the abbot to Robin's table for a forced feast. What gave the king's identity away?
answer: He pulled back his hood revealing the royal crown beneath
choices: He pulled back his hood revealing the royal crown beneath
He let slip a curse in the French of the royal court
He drew a battle scar from Acre across his cheek
Robin recognized his ring with the Plantagenet seal
context: Robin and all his men knelt before King Richard. The king pardoned them and offered Robin a place at court. Most of Robin's band followed him; he eventually missed Sherwood and returned to the forest. The Richard-pardons-Robin scene is the climax of Howard Pyle's *The Merry Adventures of Robin Hood* (1883) and most film versions.

question: Robin Hood and Little John once heard a young man weeping by the road and asked his trouble. He had stolen seven of the king's deer to feed his starving family, and the Sheriff's men had caught him. He was to be hanged that very afternoon at Nottingham gallows along with three of his brothers. Robin and his band rode at once for the gallows tree. How did they save the brothers?
answer: Robin dressed as a beggar, took the hangman's place, and cut the ropes
choices: Robin dressed as a beggar, took the hangman's place, and cut the ropes
Robin shot the hangman from the cover of a hedge
Robin bought their pardons with stolen Sheriff's gold
Robin started a forest fire that drew the guards away
context: The poaching brothers became members of Robin's band. The story is told in the ballad *Robin Hood and the Three Squires*. The Sheriff's punishment for hunting royal deer was death by hanging — the cruelty of Norman forest law drove many ordinary Englishmen into outlaw bands.

question: In one of the older Robin Hood tales, Robin Hood was wandering the forest one day when he met a young woman dressed in mail with sword and buckler at her belt. She wore a feathered cap that hid her hair. Robin, not knowing her, challenged her to single combat. They fought for an hour and neither could best the other. What revealed the stranger's identity to Robin?
answer: She lowered her sword and called him by his own true name
choices: She lowered her sword and called him by his own true name
Her cap slipped off and her long hair fell loose
She wore his own ring upon her finger
She wept and dropped her sword in surrender
context: The stranger was Maid Marian, who had disguised herself to seek Robin in Sherwood after he was outlawed. Their meeting comes from the 17th-century ballad *Robin Hood and Maid Marian*. In earlier medieval versions Robin's love is unnamed; Marian became attached to the legend through May Day mummers' plays.

question: The Sheriff of Nottingham, desperate to capture Robin Hood, once disguised himself as a wealthy butcher of Wakefield to lure Robin out. He stopped at a Sherwood inn, ate well, and spoke loudly about the fine herd of fat cattle he had to sell at fair prices. Robin Hood, learning of the merchant, came to him in disguise as a competing butcher. They struck a deal: Robin would lead the Sheriff to the best beef pasture in all England. What 'cattle' did Robin show the Sheriff?
answer: A herd of the king's own royal deer in Sherwood
choices: A herd of the king's own royal deer in Sherwood
A horde of wild boars rooting in a glade
A pack of Sherwood wolves disguised in cowhides
Robin's own men dressed in painted leather hides
context: The Sheriff fled for his life when he realized the trick — Robin and his men relieved him of his purse of three hundred pounds first. The story is in the ballad *Robin Hood and the Butcher*. Royal deer in medieval England could only be hunted by the king himself; even pointing a bow at one was a hanging crime.

question: In one of the more elaborate Robin Hood tales, King Edward held a great royal archery tournament at Finsbury Field outside London, with a golden arrow worth a hundred marks for the prize. The greatest archers in England came. Robin Hood walked in disguised as a strange archer of the north, with a black hood pulled low. The final shot was at a small willow wand stuck in the ground at three hundred paces. Robin's arrow alone struck the wand. Who recognized him afterward?
answer: The king himself, who had set the trap to find Robin
choices: The king himself, who had set the trap to find Robin
Friar Tuck, watching from the spectator stands
The Sheriff of Nottingham, by Robin's bow style
Little John, who had come dressed as a beggar
context: The king pardoned Robin again and gave him the golden arrow. Robin took his men back to Sherwood within a year — court life did not suit him. The Finsbury tournament story is in the ballad *A Gest of Robyn Hode* (c. 1450), one of the earliest extended Robin Hood texts to survive.

question: In the summer of 778 AD, Charlemagne's army was returning from a campaign in Muslim Spain. The rear-guard under the paladin Sir Roland was assigned to defend the narrow pass of Roncevaux in the Pyrenees mountains. Basque mountain warriors fell on the rear-guard at noon. Roland's loyal friend Oliver climbed to a high rock and saw the size of the enemy host — a hundred thousand men — and begged Roland to blow his ivory war-horn Olifant to call Charlemagne back to help. Why did Roland refuse?
answer: He thought it shameful to call for help while still strong
choices: He thought it shameful to call for help while still strong
He had been wounded too deeply in the lungs to blow
He had not yet sighted the enemy with his own eyes
He believed the horn was lost or stolen by the Saracens
context: In *The Song of Roland* (c. 1100), this is the central tragedy. Roland's *desmesure* — the excess of his pride — was the death of the rear-guard. Oliver and Archbishop Turpin both died at his side. Roland finally blew Olifant only when all twelve paladins were dead or dying.

question: Charlemagne (Charles the Great), King of the Franks and crowned Emperor of the Romans by Pope Leo III on Christmas Day 800 AD, was always said in the medieval romances to have surrounded himself with twelve elite knights modeled on the twelve apostles. They were called the paladins, from the Latin *palatinus* meaning 'of the palace.' The greatest of them all was Charlemagne's own nephew, who died at Roncevaux. Who was this nephew?
answer: Roland
choices: Roland
Oliver
Ogier the Dane
Turpin of Reims
context: The twelve paladins included Roland, Oliver, Archbishop Turpin, Ogier the Dane, Renaud de Montauban, Astolfo, Ganelon, Naimes, and others (lists varied). 'Paladin' came through these stories to mean any heroic champion. *The Song of Roland* (c. 1100) is the earliest major work of French literature and the founding epic of paladin-romance tradition.

question: Roland, dying at Roncevaux with the rear-guard slaughtered around him, did not want his sword to fall into Saracen hands. He had named the blade Durendal, meaning 'enduring' — and within its golden hilt were buried sacred relics: a tooth of Saint Peter, hair of Saint Denis, a thread of the Virgin Mary's robe, and a fragment of the bone of Saint Basil. Roland tried again and again to break the sword against a great marble rock. What happened to the rock and the sword?
answer: The rock split in two, the sword remained unbroken
choices: The rock split in two, the sword remained unbroken
Both the rock and Durendal shattered together
The sword sank deep into the rock and stayed there
Durendal melted from the heat of Roland's hands
context: *The Song of Roland* (c. 1100) describes Roland's three failed attempts to break Durendal. He finally lay down on a green hill, placed Olifant and Durendal beneath his body to keep them from the enemy, and died facing Spain. Charlemagne later found him in this position.

question: King Hrothgar of the Danes built a vast mead-hall called Heorot — meaning 'Hart' or 'Stag' — gilded with gold, ringed by warriors. But every night for twelve winters a monster crept down from the moors and burst into the hall, devouring sleeping warriors. The monster could not be wounded by any weapon forged by men. His descent from the line of Cain was the curse that drove him. What was his name?
answer: Grendel
choices: Grendel
Fafnir
Hrunting
Wiglaf
context: *Beowulf* survives in a single Old English manuscript copied around 1000 AD and now in the British Library. The poem describes Heorot as a meeting-place corresponding roughly to Lejre in Denmark. Heorot's name (deer/stag) suggests royal hunting symbolism — antlers were carved on its gables.

question: The Geatish prince Beowulf sailed from Sweden with fourteen warriors to help King Hrothgar of the Danes against the monster Grendel that had emptied his mead-hall Heorot. Beowulf decided to fight Grendel with no weapons or armor — since iron could not bite Grendel's hide, Beowulf would fight him bare-handed. When Grendel burst into the hall that night, Beowulf seized the monster's arm in a grip stronger than thirty men. What happened when Grendel tried to flee?
answer: His arm tore off at the shoulder
choices: His arm tore off at the shoulder
His skull split open against a doorpost
He was pinned by his hair to the wooden floor
He sank into the floor and vanished underground
context: Grendel fled to his marsh lair to die of the wound, leaving the bloody arm and shoulder in Beowulf's grip. The Danes hung the arm — and Grendel's head, brought back later from the underwater lair — in the gable of Heorot as a trophy. Heorot's name (hart, stag, antlered) and the hung arm together turned the gable into a triumph-display.

question: After Beowulf returned to Sweden from killing both Grendel and Grendel's mother at the Danish court, he served his uncle King Hygelac of the Geats faithfully for many years. Hygelac was killed raiding the Frisians. His widow Hygd offered Beowulf the throne over her young son. Beowulf refused, saying he would not take what was the boy's by right. What happened to allow Beowulf to become king at last?
answer: The young prince was killed in battle and Beowulf was then chosen
choices: The young prince was killed in battle and Beowulf was then chosen
Hygelac's widow placed the crown on him in open defiance
Beowulf overthrew the boy in single combat for the throne
The Geatish chiefs voted to set the rightful heir aside
context: Beowulf ruled the Geats peacefully for fifty winters as a wise old king. His final battle would be against a dragon that woke when a slave stole a single golden cup from its hoard. *Beowulf* survives in a single Old English manuscript of around 1000 AD and is the oldest substantial work of English literature.

question: Doctor Faustus, a learned German scholar at the University of Wittenberg, had mastered law, medicine, philosophy, and theology — but his books still left him empty. He summoned the demon Mephistopheles by drawing a magical pentagram on his study floor and reading from a forbidden grimoire. They struck a bargain: twenty-four years of any pleasure or knowledge in exchange for Faust's soul at the end. With what did Faust have to sign the contract?
answer: His own blood drawn from his arm
choices: His own blood drawn from his arm
Ink mixed with church incense
A quill made of a black raven's feather
Powdered bone from a saint's relic
context: In Christopher Marlowe's 1604 play *The Tragical History of Doctor Faustus*, Faust's blood congeals on the page as he tries to sign — a clear warning. The Latin phrase *Homo, fuge!* (Man, flee!) appears on his arm in his own blood. He ignores the sign and signs anyway. Marlowe drew on a real 16th-century German tradition about a wandering alchemist named Johann Faust.

question: The Habsburg bailiff Hermann Gessler placed his hat on a pole in Altdorf's square and ordered all who passed to bow to it. The hunter William Tell refused and was arrested. Gessler offered him freedom only if he could shoot an apple off his own son Walter's head from eighty paces with one arrow. Tell drew two arrows from his quiver, set one in his bow, slipped the other in his belt, and split the apple cleanly. Why did Tell say he had taken the second arrow?
answer: If I had killed my son, the second arrow was for you
choices: If I had killed my son, the second arrow was for you
I always carry two, one for war and one for the hunt
The second was a backup if the first broke or missed
I had vowed to my wife never to shoot only once
context: Gessler ordered Tell arrested for the threat. Tell escaped on a stormy lake crossing, hid in the mountains, and ambushed Gessler on the road to Kussnacht — killing him with that very second arrow. The William Tell legend became the founding story of Swiss independence; Friedrich Schiller's play *Wilhelm Tell* (1804) made it world-famous.

question: The Castilian knight Rodrigo Díaz de Vivar fought for both Christian and Muslim kings in the 11th-century Reconquista of Spain. He took the city of Valencia and held it as his own private kingdom. His Muslim allies addressed him in Arabic with a title meaning 'lord' or 'master', and the Christian kingdoms adapted this Arabic title into the name by which he is remembered today. What Arabic title gave him his name?
answer: Al-Sayyid (the lord)
choices: Al-Sayyid (the lord)
Al-Mansur (the victor)
Al-Faris (the rider)
Al-Hadi (the guide)
context: The Christian kingdoms adapted *al-sayyid* into *El Cid*. Rodrigo died at Valencia in 1099. The *Cantar de Mio Cid* (c. 1200) is the oldest surviving epic poem in Castilian Spanish. He was also called *El Campeador* — 'the champion' — but *El Cid* (the lord) is the title that endured. He died a natural death in Valencia after losing none of the battles he commanded.

question: The town of Hamelin in Lower Saxony was overrun with rats in 1284 AD — they swarmed the cradles, ruined the grain, poisoned the wells. A stranger in a brightly-coloured pied (multi-coloured) coat arrived at the town gate and offered to rid the town of the rats for a thousand guilders. The desperate town council agreed. The piper put a small wooden pipe to his lips and walked through the streets playing. What did the rats do?
answer: They followed him in a swarm and drowned in the River Weser
choices: They followed him in a swarm and drowned in the River Weser
They turned on each other in the streets and died fighting
They burrowed into the earth and were never seen again
They were transformed into stones along the riverbank
context: The town refused to pay the piper afterward. On Saint John's Day (June 26, 1284) the piper returned and played a different tune that drew the children instead. The story is recorded in the Hamelin town chronicles and is one of the few medieval legends with a specific dated origin. The town still has a 'Bungelosenstrasse' — Drumless Street — where no music is allowed.

question: The wizard Merlin, who would later raise Arthur and place the sword in the stone, had a strange origin. In Geoffrey of Monmouth's *History of the Kings of Britain* (c. 1136), his mother was a holy princess shut in a convent who became pregnant by no man she could name. The devils of the air had planned that one of their kind would father a child meant to be an Antichrist. But the holy baptism of the infant defeated the dark plan. What gifts did Merlin inherit?
answer: Prophecy from the demon, holiness from baptism
choices: Prophecy from the demon, holiness from baptism
Strength from his father, beauty from his mother
Magic from a fairy queen who fostered him
Knowledge of all languages of beast and bird
context: Merlin's mixed birth gave him supernatural foresight without making him evil. He would later prophesy Arthur's coming, arrange Arthur's secret birth from Uther and Igraine, and guide Arthur until imprisoned in a hawthorn tree by the enchantress Nimue (also called Vivienne). Geoffrey of Monmouth's *Prophetiae Merlini* (c. 1130) was a medieval bestseller in Britain.

question: King Uther Pendragon of Britain saw the Duchess of Cornwall, Lady Igraine, at a royal banquet and burned with love for her at once — but she was a faithful wife to Duke Gorlois, her husband. Uther made war on Cornwall to be near her. The wizard Merlin offered to use his magic to grant Uther a single night with Igraine — at a price he would name later. What did Merlin do for Uther?
answer: Changed his shape to look exactly like Igraine's husband
choices: Changed his shape to look exactly like Igraine's husband
Cast Igraine into an enchanted sleep until dawn
Sent a love potion to her wine cup at supper
Stole her image so she walked unseen to Uther's tent
context: The same night Merlin worked the spell, the real Duke Gorlois was killed in battle outside his castle. Igraine became pregnant by Uther that night; the child was Arthur, whom Merlin took at birth to be fostered in secret by Sir Ector. Merlin's price was the boy himself. The story is in Malory's *Le Morte d'Arthur* (1485) and Geoffrey of Monmouth (c. 1136).

question: The young Arthur was raised in secret by Sir Ector and his wife as a foster-son, alongside their own son who was a few years older. The older brother was a hot-tempered knight who would become Arthur's seneschal — the steward of the royal household. He was famous for his sharp tongue, his courage, and once for forgetting his sword on the day of a great tournament — sending young Arthur back to fetch it from a churchyard. What was his name?
answer: Sir Kay
choices: Sir Kay
Sir Bedivere
Sir Bors
Sir Lamorak
context: Sir Kay's forgotten sword sent Arthur to the churchyard where the sword in the stone stood. Arthur, finding the church locked, pulled the sword from the stone and gave it to Kay, who claimed for a moment that he had drawn it himself — then confessed when Ector questioned him. Kay became Arthur's seneschal and a Round Table knight, famous for sharp-tongued banter.

question: King Arthur's half-sister was a powerful enchantress raised in a nunnery where she studied the dark arts. She married King Urien of Gore but spent her years plotting against Arthur. She once stole Excalibur's enchanted scabbard while Arthur slept in her castle as a guest, and threw it into a deep lake — so that all his later wounds would bleed freely. What was her name?
answer: Morgan le Fay
choices: Morgan le Fay
Nimue of the Lake
Vivienne the Fair
Elaine of Astolat
context: Morgan le Fay was the daughter of Igraine by her first husband Duke Gorlois of Cornwall — making her Arthur's half-sister. After Camlann she was one of the three queens in the black-draped barge who came to take the dying Arthur to the island of Avalon, where she would heal him. Loving and hating Arthur in equal measure is her literary signature.

question: Sir Mordred, the traitor knight who would destroy the Round Table and kill King Arthur at the battle of Camlann, was raised at the court of King Lot of Orkney with his three loyal brothers — Sir Gawain, Sir Agravain, and Sir Gareth. But Mordred's true father was not King Lot. In Malory's *Le Morte d'Arthur*, who was Mordred's actual father?
answer: King Arthur himself, by his half-sister Morgause
choices: King Arthur himself, by his half-sister Morgause
Merlin, by an enchantment on Queen Igraine
King Uther Pendragon, by his own concubine
King Pellinore, by a maid of the Lake
context: Arthur conceived Mordred before he knew Morgause was his half-sister. When Merlin warned him that the child would destroy his kingdom, Arthur ordered all children born on May Day put adrift in a boat — a Herod-like attempt that failed when Mordred survived. Mordred's role as both nephew and son is the dark seed of the entire cycle's tragedy.

question: The night after Beowulf tore off Grendel's arm at Heorot, the monster's mother came to the mead-hall to take revenge. She seized the king's chief counselor Aeschere, killed him, and dragged his body back to the underwater lair beneath a haunted mere. King Hrothgar wept and turned to Beowulf again. The hero put on his mail-shirt and accepted a borrowed sword. Whose famous sword did Beowulf carry on the dive?
answer: Hrunting, lent to him by the Danish warrior Unferth
choices: Hrunting, lent to him by the Danish warrior Unferth
Naegling, the sword of his own grandfather Hrethel
Mimung, a Frisian blade taken from Daeghrefn
Gram, the broken sword of his ancestors
context: Unferth had earlier mocked Beowulf at the feast — claiming Beowulf had lost a swimming-match. By lending Hrunting, Unferth made peace and acknowledged Beowulf's greatness. The sword failed under the water, but the gesture was honored. Beowulf swam for nearly a day to reach the bottom of the mere.

question: Diving alone into the haunted mere to fight Grendel's mother, Beowulf was seized at the bottom by the she-monster and dragged into her underwater cave. There was light in the cave from a strange phosphorescent glow. Beowulf swung the borrowed sword Hrunting at her neck with all his strength. What happened to the sword?
answer: The famed blade failed and would not bite her
choices: The famed blade failed and would not bite her
The blade shattered against the rocks of the cave wall
The blade twisted in his hands like wet seaweed
The blade flew from his grip and lodged in the ceiling
context: Hrunting could not pierce her monster-hide. Beowulf wrestled her with his bare hands. When she nearly killed him with a long knife, his eye fell on an enormous sword hanging on the cave wall — a giant's sword from the days before the Flood. He seized it with both hands.

question: Pinned beneath Grendel's mother on the floor of her underwater cave with her dagger raised, Beowulf saw a giant ancient sword hanging on the wall — a blade forged in the days before Noah's flood, longer than any man could wield. He twisted free, seized the hilt with both hands, and swung. The blade clove through her neck. Beowulf then found the body of her dead son Grendel nearby and cut off his head as well. What happened to the giant sword?
answer: The blade melted away from the monster-blood, leaving only the hilt
choices: The blade melted away from the monster-blood, leaving only the hilt
Beowulf sank the sword into the floor of the cave forever
The blade rang like a bell and called the Geats from above
The blade rusted to red dust as he climbed from the water
context: Beowulf brought the hilt and Grendel's severed head back up to King Hrothgar's court. The melting of the blade was the burning purity of Grendel's mother's blood — a sign that the monsters were truly of the cursed line of Cain. Beowulf was rewarded with gifts and sailed home to Sweden.

question: Sir Lancelot, the greatest knight at King Arthur's court, was unaware that he had a son. Years before the Grail quest, the enchantress Brusen had used a magical illusion to make the lady Elaine of Corbenic — daughter of King Pelles — appear to Lancelot in the dark as Queen Guinevere. They spent the night together. The child of that night was raised in a convent and would become the only knight pure enough to achieve the Grail. What was the child called?
answer: Galahad
choices: Galahad
Percival
Bors
Lamorak
context: Galahad was named for one of Lancelot's own boyhood names. He arrived at Camelot as a young white-armored knight on the Feast of Pentecost, sat unharmed in the Siege Perilous, and proved his lineage by drawing the floating sword. Lancelot wept when he learned the boy was his son. Galahad would see the unveiled Grail and die in ecstasy at Sarras.

question: The Sheriff of Nottingham, beaten too often, hired a notorious mercenary outlaw-hunter named Sir Guy of Gisborne to bring Robin Hood in. Guy wore a horse-hide cloak with hooves and head still attached. He met Robin in Sherwood Forest and the two fought all afternoon. Robin slipped on a tree root and Guy seized him by the throat — but Robin called on the Virgin Mary and rallied. After Robin killed Guy, what did he do with the body?
answer: Cut off Guy's head and stuck it on his bow's tip
choices: Cut off Guy's head and stuck it on his bow's tip
Buried Guy at the base of the largest oak in Sherwood
Stripped Guy's armor and threw the body in a river
Hung Guy's body from the gallows-tree of Nottingham
context: Robin disfigured Guy's face with his Irish knife so the Sheriff would not recognize the head, then put on Guy's cloak. The Sheriff, thinking Robin Hood was dead, was tricked into letting 'Guy' enter Nottingham to rescue Little John from the dungeon. Robin then turned the bow on the Sheriff. The tale is in the ballad *Robin Hood and Guy of Gisborne*.

question: Of the three knights who together achieved the Holy Grail — Galahad, Percival, and a third — only one returned from the quest to Camelot to bear witness. He had once chosen to rescue a young woman in danger over rescuing his own brother Lionel from torture by another knight. He was the only married knight to share in the Grail vision, having been faithful to his wife despite many temptations. Who was the third Grail-knight?
answer: Sir Bors
choices: Sir Bors
Sir Tristan
Sir Kay
Sir Gawain
context: Galahad died at Sarras seeing the unveiled Grail. Percival became a hermit there and died soon after. Only Bors returned to Camelot to tell the tale. He found the Round Table half-empty when he came home — many knights had died on the quest. Bors lived to see the final fall of the kingdom at Camlann.

question: Charlemagne sent the paladin Ganelon to negotiate with the Saracen king Marsile of Saragossa in northern Spain. Ganelon was Roland's stepfather — and Roland had insulted him by suggesting his name for the dangerous mission, knowing Saracen ambassadors had been killed before. Ganelon, burning with hatred, accepted gold from Marsile in exchange for a single act. What did Ganelon promise the Saracens?
answer: He named Roland to lead Charlemagne's rear-guard
choices: He named Roland to lead Charlemagne's rear-guard
He gave the Saracens the keys to Charlemagne's tent
He pointed out the secret pass into France
He poisoned Charlemagne's morning wine cup
context: Marsile's men ambushed Roland's rear-guard at Roncevaux Pass exactly as Ganelon had arranged. When Charlemagne discovered the betrayal, Ganelon was tried — and torn apart by four horses pulling in different directions. *The Song of Roland* (c. 1100) ends with the execution. 'Ganelon' became the medieval word for traitor.

question: Roland's closest companion in Charlemagne's army was the paladin Oliver — wise, prudent, brave but not reckless. The pair complement one another in *The Song of Roland*: Oliver is sense, Roland is courage. Their famous quarrel about whether to blow Olifant was Oliver pleading reason against Roland's pride. Late in the battle at Roncevaux Pass, when both knew they were dying, what did Oliver do to Roland?
answer: Struck him a glancing blow without recognizing him through blood
choices: Struck him a glancing blow without recognizing him through blood
Cursed him with his last breath for refusing to blow Olifant
Wept on his shoulder and asked his forgiveness for cowardice
Carried him on his back to a quiet rock to die
context: Oliver, half-blinded by his own head wound, did not recognize Roland and gave him a stunning blow. Roland called to him by name, Oliver wept and asked his pardon, then died in his friend's arms. The line *Roland est preux et Olivier est sage* ('Roland is brave and Oliver is wise') summarizes the medieval pairing of courage and prudence.

question: Robin Hood and his men once stopped a group of richly-dressed travelers in Sherwood Forest and demanded their purses. The leader was an arrogant high churchman who claimed bishop's immunity. Robin, never one to spare a fat priest, made the bishop sing high mass over an outdoor altar of moss and pine needles before letting him go. The bishop also had to do something embarrassing with his own horse. What was it?
answer: Dance a jig hand-in-hand with Friar Tuck around the altar
choices: Dance a jig hand-in-hand with Friar Tuck around the altar
Climb up backwards and ride into Nottingham facing the tail
Lead the horse blindfolded into a Sherwood mud-pit
Beg the horse aloud to forgive him his hard riding
context: The ballad *Robin Hood and the Bishop of Hereford* mixes piety and mockery — Robin kept the bishop's gold but made him keep his churchly office honestly while a guest at the outlaws' fire. The Bishop of Hereford in medieval England was the wealthiest bishopric outside Canterbury, drawing Robin's particular dislike.

question: Sir Tristan of the Round Table came from a small Cornish kingdom across a narrow stretch of water from Cornwall's mainland — a kingdom said in the medieval romances to have sunk beneath the sea in a single night, drowning a hundred and forty churches and the noble seat of King Mark. What was this lost kingdom called?
answer: Lyonesse
choices: Lyonesse
Logres
Listenoise
Lothian
context: The legend may preserve a folk memory of Cornish coastal land lost to rising seas at the end of the last Ice Age. The Isles of Scilly off the Cornish coast were once connected by a single landmass, now submerged. Tennyson's *Idylls of the King* used Lyonesse as the place where Arthur's final battle was fought.

question: Lancelot, once driven from Camelot in disgrace after Queen Guinevere thought he had been unfaithful to her with the lady Elaine of Corbenic, fled into the wilderness in a fit of madness. For two years he wandered the forests of Britain naked and wild-haired, eating berries, fighting off other beggars, speaking to no one. By what means was Lancelot eventually healed?
answer: The Grail was held over him as he slept
choices: The Grail was held over him as he slept
A hermit lit incense beside him for nine nights
Sir Galahad found him and called his true name
King Arthur prayed at the holy well of Canterbury
context: Found unconscious in a cottage garden, Lancelot was carried to the Grail Castle of Corbenic where his son Galahad lived. The Grail was held over him until he woke clear-minded. Healed, he returned to Camelot — and to Guinevere. The Grail's healing of the man whose adultery had grieved Heaven is one of the great paradoxes of the Lancelot cycle.

question: Robin Hood once met a young minstrel walking through Sherwood weeping bitterly. He learned the lad's name was Allan a Dale and that his true love was to be married that very afternoon — but to a wealthy old knight, not to him. The girl's father had refused to consider a poor harp-player. Robin and his men rode to the church and arrived just as the wedding was beginning. How did Robin force the marriage to change?
answer: He took the bishop's place at the altar and married them
choices: He took the bishop's place at the altar and married them
He shot the old knight from the church door with his bow
He kidnapped the bride and rode back to Sherwood with her
He paid the father a great purse of gold for the daughter
context: Robin Hood asked Allan and his sweetheart whether they consented — they did — then declared them married in his outlaw's voice. The Bishop of Hereford, who had been about to perform the wrongful match, was sent home in mockery. Allan a Dale became Sherwood's chief minstrel and writer of the band's ballads.

question: On the Feast of Pentecost at Camelot, the empty seat at the Round Table called the Siege Perilous — bordered in gold and inscribed with a deadly warning — had been waiting for one hundred and fifty years. Merlin had prophesied that any unworthy knight sitting in it would be swallowed by the earth or burst into flame, and that only the destined Grail-knight could ever take the seat. That morning a young knight in white armor rode into the court with an old hermit. The hermit named him as the awaited one. The boy walked through the staring court, knelt before Arthur, and sat down in the Siege Perilous without harm. What appeared at the Round Table that very evening?
answer: A veiled vision of the Holy Grail moving through the hall
choices: A veiled vision of the Holy Grail moving through the hall
A second floating stone with a sword for the new knight
A vast white hart Arthur was bound to follow alone
A wounded swan bearing a letter from Avalon
context: The young knight was Sir Galahad, Lancelot's son. After the Grail vision passed all the knights vowed to seek it — a vow that emptied Camelot of its greatest warriors and began the slow ruin of the Round Table. Galahad would be the only one to see the unveiled Grail; he died in ecstasy at the vision in the city of Sarras.

question: King Arthur's traitor nephew Sir Mordred had long resented his uncle's favor of Sir Lancelot. With his loyal friend Sir Agravain — Gawain's hot-tempered brother — Mordred laid a trap to expose the queen and her lover. One night while Arthur was away on a hunt, Mordred and twelve other knights surrounded Queen Guinevere's chamber where Lancelot had visited her. They called out his name and demanded he surrender. Lancelot was unarmed except for his sword. Agravain and the twelve others were armed and in full mail. What did Lancelot do?
answer: Killed all twelve attackers and escaped, leaving Mordred alone wounded
choices: Killed all twelve attackers and escaped, leaving Mordred alone wounded
Surrendered to face Arthur's justice as a true knight ought to do
Took his own life with his sword rather than be taken alive
Fled out a window, leaving Guinevere to be condemned alone
context: Mordred ran straight to King Arthur with the news. Arthur, bound by his own laws, was forced to sentence Guinevere to burn at the stake for treason. Lancelot rescued her from the flames at the last moment but in the chaos killed Sir Gareth and Sir Gaheris — Gawain's beloved younger brothers — who had refused to bear arms. Gawain's grief turned to relentless hatred, dragging Arthur into civil war with Lancelot.

question: King Arthur was forced by his own laws to sentence Queen Guinevere to burn at the stake at Carlisle for treason after Sir Mordred's evidence of her affair with Sir Lancelot. The pyre was built in the meadow outside the city; the queen was led to the stake in her white smock; the torch was raised. From the woods on every side Sir Lancelot and his small loyal company burst out at full gallop. Lancelot cut down the executioners and the guard, lifted Guinevere onto his horse, and galloped for the safety of his castle Joyous Gard. But in the chaos he had killed two knights who had refused to fight him because they loved him. Whose two brothers were they?
answer: Sir Gawain's two younger brothers Gareth and Gaheris
choices: Sir Gawain's two younger brothers Gareth and Gaheris
Sir Bors's two cousins Lionel and Ector de Maris
Sir Tristan's two foster-brothers Sagramore and Lamorak
Sir Percival's two stepbrothers Aglovale and Tor
context: Gareth and Gaheris had attended the burning unarmed because Arthur ordered it, but Lancelot did not see them in the press. Gawain — who had once loved Lancelot like a brother — swore vengeance. The civil war between Arthur (driven by Gawain) and Lancelot was the gap that gave Mordred his chance to seize the throne while Arthur was campaigning across the sea in France.

question: The wizard Merlin, who had raised King Arthur, placed the sword in the stone, and built Stonehenge, fell at last in his old age into a foolish love for a young enchantress called Nimue (or Vivienne in some versions) — the Damsel of the Lake. He taught her his secret arts, hoping to win her affection. She used the teaching against him. According to Malory's *Le Morte d'Arthur*, by what means did Vivienne finally trap Merlin so that no one could ever rescue him?
answer: Sealed him under a great stone using his own enchantment of locking
choices: Sealed him under a great stone using his own enchantment of locking
Bound him at the bottom of the lake in chains of silver
Trapped him in a glass tower whose walls reflected only himself
Burned him alive in a hawthorn hedge of her conjuring
context: In Geoffrey of Monmouth's *Vita Merlini* and the French *Vulgate Cycle*, Merlin is variously imprisoned in a cave of crystal, a hawthorn tree, or under a great stone. Malory chose the stone. Merlin foresaw his own doom and warned Arthur about it — but did nothing to prevent it. Without his counsel the Round Table would slowly unravel.

question: After the vision of the veiled Grail moved through the Round Table on the night Galahad arrived, every knight in Camelot vowed to ride forth on the Quest of the Holy Grail. King Arthur wept at the news. He knew that many of those knights would never return — and that the kingdom would weaken in their absence. Of all the Round Table knights, four made the deepest progress in the quest. Galahad, Percival, and Bors were three. Who was the fourth — the one whose adulterous love kept him from seeing the Grail unveiled?
answer: Sir Lancelot
choices: Sir Lancelot
Sir Gawain
Sir Kay
Sir Bedivere
context: Lancelot, blocked by his sin with Guinevere, was permitted a single glimpse of the Grail through a half-open door — and was struck down with a vision so dazzling he could not rise for many days. Of the four, Galahad alone saw the unveiled Grail and died in ecstasy. Bors alone returned to Camelot.

question: King Arthur once stopped to rest at the castle of his half-sister Morgan le Fay — Morgan the enchantress, who hated him for his choice of Guinevere over her own preferred candidate, and who plotted constantly against the Round Table. Arthur slept in a guest chamber with Excalibur on a stand beside him and the enchanted scabbard at his hip. He woke at dawn to find both gone. Morgan was found near a deep lake holding the scabbard high. What did she do with it?
answer: She threw it into the lake so it could never be recovered
choices: She threw it into the lake so it could never be recovered
She forged it into a crown for her son Yvain
She buried it beneath her own bed for safe keeping
She melted it down and sold the gold to passing merchants
context: Without the scabbard, Arthur's later wounds would bleed freely. Morgan had been waiting for the chance for years. She replaced Excalibur with a counterfeit sword (returning the real Excalibur only on later threat from the Lady of the Lake), but the scabbard was lost forever to the lake. The wound Mordred eventually gave Arthur at Camlann thus bled — and Arthur died from it.

question: Sir Gawain, Arthur's eldest sister-son and the third-greatest knight of Camelot after Lancelot and Galahad, was wounded twice in the head by Lancelot during the civil war that Gawain's own hatred had forced upon them. Lancelot had spared his life both times. As Arthur and Gawain pursued Lancelot into France, Mordred seized the throne in Britain. Arthur and Gawain rushed home. As Arthur's army landed at Dover, the head-wound burst open again as Gawain fought to clear the beach. Knowing he was dying, Gawain dictated a letter. To whom did he write?
answer: To Sir Lancelot, begging forgiveness and asking him to come
choices: To Sir Lancelot, begging forgiveness and asking him to come
To Queen Guinevere, with a parting gift and his blessing
To Merlin in his stone tomb, asking for a final prophecy
To his mother Morgause, naming Mordred his murderer
context: Gawain's deathbed letter to Lancelot — full of remorse for the hatred that had broken the Round Table — is one of the most moving moments in Malory. Lancelot arrived at Dover too late to see him alive. He knelt at Gawain's tomb and wept for two days. Gawain's mortal wound was the price of the civil war that opened Britain to Mordred.

question: After the catastrophic Battle of Camlann had ended in mutual destruction, the mortally-wounded King Arthur was carried from the field by his last knight, Sir Bedivere. Beside a misty lake a black-draped barge appeared, rowed by three queens who wept as they took the king on board. According to Malory, who were the three queens?
answer: Morgan le Fay, the Queen of Northgalis, and the Queen of the Waste Lands
choices: Morgan le Fay, the Queen of Northgalis, and the Queen of the Waste Lands
Guinevere, Iseult of Ireland, and Lady Lyonors of the Castle
Vivienne of the Lake, Elaine of Astolat, and Lynette
Saint Brigid, Saint Hilda, and the Abbess of Glastonbury
context: Despite her old hatred of Arthur, Morgan le Fay — his half-sister enchantress — was named first of the three queens who came to take him to Avalon. The barge slipped into the mist and Bedivere never saw it again. Arthur was said in some traditions to lie healing on the island and to return when Britain's hour of need was greatest — *Rex quondam, rexque futurus*, the once and future king.

question: After King Arthur's death at Camlann, Queen Guinevere took the veil at the abbey of Amesbury — a Benedictine convent — and lived out her remaining years as the abbess, weeping daily for the kingdom her love had helped destroy. Sir Lancelot, having heard of her retreat, came at last to see her one final time. She refused even to embrace him. What did she ask him to do?
answer: To leave her, never seek her again, and pray for her soul
choices: To leave her, never seek her again, and pray for her soul
To take her secretly across the sea to his castle in France
To kill her with his own sword and bury her quickly
To bring her Arthur's body for honor at Glastonbury Abbey
context: Lancelot honored her wish. He took monastic vows at Glastonbury Abbey under the holy hermit who had been Archbishop of Canterbury. When Guinevere died at Amesbury seven years later, Lancelot and seven brother-monks walked to fetch her body. She was buried beside Arthur. Lancelot died within six weeks from grief, and was buried at Joyous Gard.

question: Sir Tristan and Iseult had loved each other through the magical love-potion drunk on the voyage to Cornwall, where Iseult was to wed Tristan's uncle King Mark. Years of secret meetings and forced separations followed. In the romance version closest to Wagner's opera, Mark eventually caught them together in the orchard. He had sworn to kill them with his own hand. How did Tristan finally die?
answer: Stabbed in the back by King Mark with a poisoned spear
choices: Stabbed in the back by King Mark with a poisoned spear
Drowned in the Cornish sea after a long sword duel
Beheaded at sunrise on the cliff above Tintagel
Killed in tournament by his own foster-brother Kahedin
context: In some versions Tristan dies away from Cornwall, in Brittany, of a wound from a poisoned spear in battle. In others King Mark himself kills him from behind in the orchard. Iseult of Ireland dies of grief beside Tristan's body. King Mark planted a rose bush over Tristan's grave and a vine over Iseult's — they grew together and intertwined no matter how often he cut them apart.

question: After King Arthur was mortally wounded by his nephew Sir Mordred at the Battle of Camlann, the dying king ordered his last surviving knight Sir Bedivere to throw the sword Excalibur back into the lake — for the sword had come from the lake and must return there before he died. Bedivere walked to the water carrying Excalibur and looked at its golden hilt set with precious stones. Twice he could not bring himself to do it. What lie did Bedivere tell Arthur on his return?
answer: That he had thrown it and saw only the waves
choices: That he had thrown it and saw only the waves
That a fisherman had stolen it from his hand
That the lake had frozen solid before his eyes
That a dragon had risen from the lake to take it
context: Arthur knew Bedivere lied — for if Excalibur had truly entered the water, marvelous things should have happened. After being sent back a third time, Bedivere finally obeyed. A pale arm clothed in white samite rose from the lake and caught Excalibur, brandished it three times, and drew it down into the depths. The sword was returned. Then the three queens came in their barge for Arthur.

question: Of the four knights who pressed deepest into the Quest of the Holy Grail — Galahad, Percival, Bors, and Lancelot — only one was pure enough to see the Grail unveiled. The three pure knights eventually came to a holy ship that bore them across the sea to the eastern city of Sarras. There Joseph of Arimathea himself appeared in a vision and celebrated a mass at the Grail. Galahad was permitted to look directly into the holy vessel. What happened to him at the vision?
answer: He died in ecstasy with his soul lifted up to heaven
choices: He died in ecstasy with his soul lifted up to heaven
He was made immortal as the eternal guardian of the Grail
He returned to Camelot with the Grail set on a high altar
He was sent back to find Arthur and heal the wasteland
context: The 13th-century *Queste del Saint Graal* describes Galahad's death as the kind of perfect ending a saint might envy. Percival became a hermit at Sarras and died within a year of grief; Bors alone returned to Camelot to tell Arthur the story. The Grail itself was carried up to heaven with Galahad's soul; it has never been seen on earth since.

question: King Arthur and Sir Gawain crossed the English Channel with the bulk of the Round Table's remaining knights to besiege Sir Lancelot in his fortress Joyous Gard in northern France, in the bitter civil war following Lancelot's killing of Gawain's brothers. Arthur left his nephew Sir Mordred as regent of Britain in his absence. Mordred, the secret son Arthur had fathered on his half-sister Morgause, seized his chance. He produced forged letters reporting Arthur dead in France and called the British barons together at London. What did he demand of Queen Guinevere?
answer: That she marry him at once to make his crown lawful
choices: That she marry him at once to make his crown lawful
That she resign her rank and enter the Tower as a captive
That she swear allegiance to him before Arthur's body returned
That she sail at once to her father's old kingdom of Cameliard
context: Guinevere fled to the Tower of London and fortified herself, refusing the marriage. Mordred laid siege to her there until the news reached Arthur in France. Arthur abandoned the siege of Joyous Gard immediately and raced home. The two armies — Arthur with what was left of the Round Table; Mordred with British rebels and Saxon mercenaries — met on Salisbury Plain at Camlann.

question: On a Whitsuntide morning, a tall handsome young man arrived at Camelot, kept his name secret, and asked King Arthur for three boons — but only one to be granted at once. The first was food and drink for a year in the king's kitchen. Sir Kay, mocking him for his pretty hands and untrained look, gave him the kitchen nickname *Beaumains*, meaning 'beautiful hands' in French. A year later the man appeared at court fully grown and asked the other two boons — to undertake a quest, and to be knighted by Lancelot. Who was Beaumains?
answer: Sir Gareth, the youngest brother of Sir Gawain
choices: Sir Gareth, the youngest brother of Sir Gawain
Sir Lamorak, the son of King Pellinore
Sir Palamedes, the Saracen knight of Cornwall
Sir Aglovale, Sir Percival's elder brother
context: Sir Gareth had wanted to win his rank by his own deeds, not by his royal blood. Lancelot knighted him gladly. Gareth went on the quest, rescued Lady Lyonesse (despite being scolded the whole way by her sister Lynette), defeated four colored knights of the cardinal directions, and married Lyonesse. He was one of the two brothers Lancelot accidentally killed at Guinevere's rescue from the stake — turning Gawain forever against Lancelot.

question: Sir Percival's father had been killed in battle along with his older brothers. His mother, terrified of losing her last child to the dangers of chivalry, raised him alone in a deep Welsh forest, hiding all knowledge of knights and weapons from him. One day a band of knights in shining armor rode through the forest hunting and the boy saw them for the first time. He thought they must be angels. He set off to follow them to King Arthur's court. What was his mother's fate?
answer: She died of grief on the road shortly after he left
choices: She died of grief on the road shortly after he left
She entered a convent and became a famous abbess
She poisoned herself with the same fire that killed her sons
She followed him in disguise and became his squire
context: Percival's encounter with the knights and his innocent following of them is one of the foundational scenes of the Grail romance. In Chrétien de Troyes' *Perceval* (c. 1180), his mother dies of grief at the moment he leaves home — and Percival's failure to ask the right question at the Grail Castle is partly attributed to his guilt over this. He returns years later to ask the question and earn the Grail.

question: Old, sick with a long fever, and grown weak in body but still strong in heart, Robin Hood rode with his old friend Little John to Kirklees Priory in Yorkshire — a Cistercian convent run by his own cousin the Prioress, who was famed throughout England as a healer. The medieval treatment for fever was bloodletting. Robin asked the Prioress to bleed him to break the fever. She agreed and took him to a high chamber. What did the Prioress do to Robin?
answer: She opened the vein and let it run until his blood was gone
choices: She opened the vein and let it run until his blood was gone
She gave him a goblet of yew-bark poison disguised as broth
She suffocated him in his sickbed with a heavy cloak
She locked him in a chapel until he starved at the altar
context: The Prioress, secretly the lover of the wicked Sir Roger of Doncaster, betrayed Robin for the bounty on his head — opening the vein wide and locking the door. By the time Little John heard the cries it was too late. Robin's death at Kirklees Priory by treachery of his own cousin appears in the 15th-century ballad *A Gest of Robyn Hode* and in nearly every later telling.

question: Dying in the high chamber at Kirklees Priory from the Prioress's treacherous bleeding, Robin Hood roused himself once more when Little John finally broke in through the door. Robin asked Little John for two things — first to spare the Prioress and her women (he would not have an old man's blood-vengeance), and second to bring him his longbow and a single arrow. Robin lay in the bed too weak to draw it. He fitted the arrow and asked Little John to open the window. What did Robin ask Little John to do with where the arrow fell?
answer: Bury me where this arrow lands
choices: Bury me where this arrow lands
Carry me out to that very tree to die
Burn this house to ashes around my body
Lay an arrow on each grave of Sherwood's dead
context: Robin's last arrow flew through the window and lodged in the trunk of a tree several hundred yards away — the strength of even his dying shot. Little John buried him there with his bow and quiver. The legendary site at Kirklees Park in West Yorkshire still has a stone reputed to mark Robin's grave. The ballad of Robin's death is one of the oldest in the cycle, appearing first in *A Gest of Robyn Hode* (c. 1450).

question: Disguised as a wandering shepherd, Robin Hood once arrived at a great fair in the town of Wentbridge in Yorkshire to watch the wrestling matches and the bear-baiting. The Sheriff's prize wrestler — a massive butcher's son from York — had thrown every challenger. Robin, who had been a champion wrestler in his youth, stepped into the ring. What was the prize Robin won?
answer: A great white bull, a saddle, and a pair of golden spurs
choices: A great white bull, a saddle, and a pair of golden spurs
A purse of fifty silver pennies and a gilt drinking horn
A new green cloak and a fine longbow of yew wood
A fat ox, a barrel of ale, and the freedom of the town
context: Robin gave the bull and the prizes to the poor cottagers around the fair before the Sheriff could recognize him and seize him. The wrestling-match ballad is a small but characteristic Robin Hood story — the outlaw winning a prize honestly and then disposing of it in pure generosity to the poor, with no theft involved at all. It survives in the ballad *Robin Hood and the Tanner*.

question: When Robin Hood had been outlawed and forced into Sherwood Forest, his betrothed lady Maid Marian could not endure being parted from him. She cut her long hair, put on a young squire's mail and surcoat, took up sword and buckler, and rode alone into Sherwood searching for him. In one telling, she met Robin himself — who did not recognize her. They fought for over an hour and neither could overcome the other. How did Robin learn the stranger's identity?
answer: He recognized her voice when she called out for mercy
choices: He recognized her voice when she called out for mercy
Her helmet was knocked off and her hair fell down
His shot snapped her sword and she swore in her own voice
She wore his ring on a chain visible through her surcoat
context: Robin and Marian embraced laughing in the Sherwood glade and rode back to camp together. The 17th-century ballad *Robin Hood and Maid Marian* dramatizes the scene fully — Marian had become attached to the Robin Hood legend through May Day mummers' plays, where the May Queen was always partnered with the man playing Robin Hood.

question: Robin Hood once disguised himself as an old beggar and walked into Nottingham on a market day, hoping to learn what new plot the Sheriff had hatched against the band in Sherwood. He sat by the road eating bread and cheese. Three of the Sheriff's foresters rode by and stopped to make sport of him. They challenged the old beggar to a shooting match for a prize of three of the king's deer. Robin agreed — the deer were already his to give. What did Robin do when the foresters realized whom they had been mocking?
answer: Took their bows and arrows and sent them home in their shirts
choices: Took their bows and arrows and sent them home in their shirts
Shot them dead one after the other with their own arrows
Tied them all three to a great oak overnight for the wolves
Sold them as bondsmen to a passing tinker for three pence
context: The story survives in the ballad *Robin Hood's Progress to Nottingham*. Foresters in medieval England — appointed by the king to enforce the harsh Forest Law that forbade ordinary peasants from hunting deer or even gathering firewood in royal forests — were among the most hated officials in the countryside. Robin's humiliation of them was a small public victory for the poor.

question: On a Sherwood path one morning Robin Hood met a young man dressed in a bright red doublet of silk, his hair set in fashionable curls, walking along singing softly. Robin demanded his purse. The stranger threw off his red doublet, drew a long sword, and challenged Robin to combat. They fought on the path for an hour without either gaining the advantage. What was the stranger's name?
answer: Will Scarlet, a long-lost nephew of Robin Hood
choices: Will Scarlet, a long-lost nephew of Robin Hood
Will Stutely, the king's chief forester's son
Will Cloudesley, the famous archer of the north
Will Wakefield, a wealthy wool merchant from York
context: Will Scarlet — sometimes called Will Scathlock or Will Scarlock in older ballads — was Robin's nephew, the son of his elder sister. He had grown up in luxury but came to Sherwood to find his uncle after his estate was confiscated by King John. Scarlet became one of Robin's most reliable swordsmen, known for the bright red clothes that gave him his name. He appears in the 15th-century *Gest of Robyn Hode*.

question: In Sherwood Forest there grew an enormous oak tree, hundreds of years old, with a trunk so wide eight men holding hands could just encircle it. Robin Hood and his band used the great hollow trunk as a hiding-place when the Sheriff's men passed by in the forest. The tree still stands in modern Sherwood Forest near the village of Edwinstowe — propped up now with steel supports, said to be a thousand years old. What is this tree commonly called today?
answer: The Major Oak
choices: The Major Oak
The Sheriff's Bane
The Sherwood King
The Robin's Tree
context: The Major Oak is in Birklands, part of Sherwood Forest in Nottinghamshire, England. Its trunk is about 11 meters in circumference. The name 'Major Oak' is from Major Hayman Rooke, an 18th-century antiquary who included the tree in a book of ancient Nottinghamshire oaks. Whether it is truly the tree where Robin Hood hid is unverifiable but the legend has clung to it for centuries.

question: After meeting Robin Hood in Sherwood Forest, the disguised King Richard the Lionheart was so impressed by Robin's company that he revealed his identity and offered Robin and his men a royal pardon. Robin knelt in the leaf-mould before the king. The pardon required Robin to give up Sherwood and come to live at the royal court in London — a place Robin found stifling within months. What did Robin Hood eventually do?
answer: Begged leave to return to Sherwood and went back to his outlaw life
choices: Begged leave to return to Sherwood and went back to his outlaw life
Married a court lady and lived as a wealthy baron near London
Joined Richard on the Third Crusade to the Holy Land
Was poisoned by the jealous Sheriff of Nottingham at a feast
context: Most Robin Hood ballads agree that Robin could not endure court life. He returned to Sherwood and resumed living outside the law — though usually treated by sheriffs after that as a tolerated nuisance rather than a hunted criminal. In the ballad *A Gest of Robyn Hode* he survives in Sherwood another twenty-two years before his death at Kirklees Priory.

question: When Robin Hood first met the fighting friar of Fountains Dale (later called Friar Tuck), they tested each other with quarterstaves at his hermitage on the bank of the River Skell. Tuck was a stout cheerful man who could match Little John for size and pure strength. Robin and Tuck fought for half a day on the bank, then in the river itself, and finally on the far side soaking wet. Neither won. What did Robin offer Tuck to settle the matter?
answer: A place in Sherwood with a free hand to drink and feast
choices: A place in Sherwood with a free hand to drink and feast
Half of Robin's purse and the title of band's confessor
A quarter of every haul taken on the road through Sherwood
Robin's own quarterstaff and a green Sherwood archer's cap
context: Friar Tuck became Sherwood's chaplain and chief drinker. His historical inspiration may have been a real Sussex chaplain named Robert Stafford who in the 1410s called himself 'Frere Tuk' while leading a small outlaw band. The literary Tuck became fixed through 16th-century May Games and ballads like *Robin Hood and the Curtal Friar*.

question: The Sheriff of Nottingham — the great chief enemy of Robin Hood in the ballads — was killed by Robin in one of the final stories of their long contest. After the Sheriff broke a safe-conduct given to Robin Hood and tried to capture him at a banquet in Nottingham, Robin escaped, gathered his men, and returned to find the Sheriff. How did Robin Hood kill the Sheriff?
answer: Cut off his head with the Sheriff's own sword on the road
choices: Cut off his head with the Sheriff's own sword on the road
Shot him through a window of Nottingham Castle with one arrow
Drowned him in the Trent River from a small boat
Hanged him from a Sherwood oak with his own girdle
context: Different ballads tell the death of the Sheriff differently. In *Robin Hood and Guy of Gisborne*, Robin kills the Sheriff with his own sword on the road. In *A Gest of Robyn Hode*, he is shot through the heart with a single arrow. He was the bank's archetypal greedy, treacherous, oath-breaking official — the embodiment of unjust forest law and Norman oppression of Saxons in popular memory.

question: All twelve of Charlemagne's paladins were dead at the Pass of Roncevaux in the summer of 778 AD. Roland alone still stood, wounded in many places. He had refused so long to blow the great ivory war-horn Olifant — his sole means of summoning Charlemagne and the main army back across the mountains — that the rear-guard had been wiped out around him. At last he set Olifant to his lips and blew with all his remaining strength. He blew it three times. What happened to Roland at the third blast?
answer: The veins in his temples burst and blood ran from his eyes
choices: The veins in his temples burst and blood ran from his eyes
His armor cracked open across his ribs from the effort
His teeth shattered against the ivory mouthpiece in his throat
The horn split lengthwise from rim to bell with a single crack
context: Charlemagne, riding far ahead in France with the main host, heard the third blast across thirty miles and turned back at once — but he arrived at Roncevaux too late. He found Roland dead on a green hill, lying on his back with his face turned toward Spain so he could die unrepentant facing the enemy. *The Song of Roland* (c. 1100) describes the bursting veins exactly.

question: When Charlemagne arrived at the Pass of Roncevaux too late to save his rear-guard, he found Roland dead on a green hill with Olifant and Durendal beneath him. The Saracen army that had ambushed Roland was already retreating across the mountains into Spain. Charlemagne knelt and prayed for vengeance — and the sun stood still in the sky to give him time to pursue. He chased the Saracens all the way back to Saragossa and besieged it. What was the fate of the traitor Ganelon, the stepfather of Roland who had arranged the ambush?
answer: Pulled apart by four horses tied to his arms and legs
choices: Pulled apart by four horses tied to his arms and legs
Hanged from a great oak at the gates of Paris
Sent to die as a slave at the silver mines of Almaden
Walled up alive in a tower for forty years of fasting
