context: Ganelon's execution by being torn apart between four horses is one of the most graphic punishments in medieval literature. The trial at Aachen ended with the verdict only after Ganelon's champion Pinabel was killed in single combat by Charlemagne's own champion Thierry. *The Song of Roland* (c. 1100) describes the execution. Ganelon's name became the medieval word for traitor.

question: Charlemagne, the great King of the Franks who had united most of western and central Europe under one Christian rule, attended Christmas Mass at the basilica of Saint Peter in Rome on December 25, 800 AD. According to the chronicler Einhard, who later wrote a biography of the emperor, Pope Leo III placed a crown on Charlemagne's head as he rose from prayer, and the Roman people acclaimed him with a triple shout. What was the formal title Charlemagne received that day?
answer: Imperator Romanorum — Emperor of the Romans
choices: Imperator Romanorum — Emperor of the Romans
Augustus Pannoniae — Augustus of the Western Lands
Rex Francorum et Magnus — Great King of the Franks
Servus Apostolicus — Servant of the Apostolic See
context: The shout of the people was *Carolo Augusto, a Deo coronato, magno et pacifico imperatori Romanorum, vita et victoria!* — 'To Charles Augustus, crowned by God, great and peaceful emperor of the Romans, life and victory!' This was the symbolic founding of the Holy Roman Empire that would last in name until 1806. Einhard reports Charlemagne later complained he would never have entered the church that day if he had known what was about to happen.

question: Roland's great war-horn Olifant — the name comes from the Latin *olifantum* meaning 'elephant' — was an enormous spiral hunting-horn carved from a single elephant tusk and reinforced with gold and jewels. The horn could be heard for thirty miles when blown by a powerful man. Roland refused to blow it when the rear-guard was first ambushed at Roncevaux. By the time he finally blew it, his strength was failing and most of the paladins had died. Where did Roland set Olifant when he himself lay dying?
answer: He laid it beneath his body to keep it from the Saracens
choices: He laid it beneath his body to keep it from the Saracens
He hurled it down a deep ravine in the pass
He gave it to Archbishop Turpin to carry to safety
He sounded it once more from a high rock-spire
context: Roland placed Olifant and Durendal beneath his body together. Charlemagne found him in that position lying on his back facing south toward Spain — unrepentant, refusing to die facing his own kingdom. Several medieval cathedrals later claimed to display the actual Olifant; the most famous example, of unclear provenance, is the so-called 'Roland's horn' kept at the Cathedral of Aix-la-Chapelle (Aachen).

question: The morning after Grendel had fled bleeding from Heorot with his arm torn off, Grendel's monstrous mother came in the night to take vengeance — killing King Hrothgar's chief counselor Aeschere and dragging him back to her underwater lair beneath a haunted mere. Beowulf vowed to follow. The mere was so deep that warriors said no man had ever touched its bottom and lived. Beowulf put on his mail-shirt, borrowed the famous sword Hrunting from Unferth, and dived. He swam down for the better part of a day. What was the cave he discovered at the bottom?
answer: A dry chamber lit by an eerie glow with a high rocky roof
choices: A dry chamber lit by an eerie glow with a high rocky roof
A shallow drowned hall full of skeletons and seaweed
A tunnel that ran through the mountain to the open sea
A black grotto with no light except his own armor's gleam
context: Grendel's mother seized Beowulf at the bottom of the mere and dragged him through her cave. The cave was dry — a chamber within a chamber, lit by a phosphorescent glow that may be an early literary glimpse of natural cave luminescence. Hrunting failed against her hide; Beowulf saved his life only with a giant's sword he found hanging on the wall.

question: Having killed Grendel's mother in her underwater cave with the giant's sword hanging on the wall, Beowulf saw the body of her dead son Grendel laid out nearby. He cut off Grendel's head as a trophy and prepared to swim back up to the surface — a journey of many hours. The blade of the giant's sword had already melted from the monster's blood, leaving only the heavy hilt. What did Beowulf carry up to the surface of the mere?
answer: Grendel's severed head and the giant sword's bare hilt
choices: Grendel's severed head and the giant sword's bare hilt
Grendel's mother's severed arm and her dagger
A cup of treasure-gold from the cave floor
Aeschere's body wrapped in his own war-cloak
context: Beowulf needed four Geats to drag Grendel's head from the mere onto the bank — it was that large. The hilt of the giant's sword was returned to King Hrothgar as a wonder; runes engraved on it told the story of the giants destroyed by Noah's flood. Beowulf was richly rewarded and sailed home to Sweden with gifts of horses, gold, and weapons.

question: Beowulf had ruled the Geats of southern Sweden as a wise old king for fifty winters when a slave hiding in a barrow stole a single golden cup from an enormous treasure hoard. The dragon that had brooded over the hoard for three centuries woke in fury and began burning Geatish farms and villages, even Beowulf's own great hall. The old king, now grey and stiff with age, took up his iron shield and went out to fight the dragon at the barrow. Of his hand-picked companions, how many stayed with him during the fight?
answer: Only the young kinsman Wiglaf out of twelve picked men
choices: Only the young kinsman Wiglaf out of twelve picked men
Twelve sworn warriors, his oldest battle-companions
All of his court but the dragon killed them quickly
None at all even his closest hearth-companions fled
context: Beowulf's other companions fled in terror when the dragon's fire-breath struck. Only the young warrior Wiglaf — Beowulf's young kinsman — stood by him. Together they killed the dragon: Beowulf with his great knife to the belly, Wiglaf striking the throat. But Beowulf was bitten in the neck and the dragon's venom worked into him. He died as the dragon died.

question: Beowulf died of the dragon's venom shortly after the killing of the dragon. Before he died he made his young kinsman Wiglaf inherit the kingdom and gave instructions about the burial. He wanted his ashes laid on the headland called Hronesness — meaning 'Whale-Headland' — so that sailors at sea would always see his grave-mound. What was built over Beowulf's pyre?
answer: A vast mound visible from far out at sea
choices: A vast mound visible from far out at sea
A stone hall in the shape of his Geatish ring-hall
A wooden ship dragged uphill from the harbor
An iron chest sealed with the dragon's last fang
context: The dragon's cursed treasure was buried with Beowulf — the cowardly companions who fled the dragon were too ashamed to claim any of it. Twelve picked warriors rode around the burning pyre singing his praises and weeping. The poem *Beowulf* survives in a single Old English manuscript from around 1000 AD, copied by two scribes — the last lines of the poem describe him as *manna mildust ond monðwærust, leodum liðost ond lofgeornost* — gentlest of men, most gracious, kindest to his people, and most eager for fame.

question: Doctor Faustus signed Mephistopheles's contract in his own blood from his arm — twenty-four years of service in exchange for his soul. As he wrote, the blood congealed thickly so the pen would not move. Mephistopheles brought a brazier of glowing coals to warm and thin the blood. As the contract was completed, two words appeared inscribed on Faust's own forearm in his own blood. The Latin meant 'Man, flee!'. What was the Latin?
answer: Homo, fuge!
choices: Homo, fuge!
Memento mori!
Pacta sunt servanda!
Vade retro, Satana!
context: In Christopher Marlowe's *Doctor Faustus* (1604), Faust sees the warning *Homo, fuge!* on his arm and tries briefly to repent. Mephistopheles distracts him with shows of devils dancing and a parade of the Seven Deadly Sins. Faust signs anyway. The Latin warning is a direct quotation from the Faust chapbook of 1587 — the legend that Marlowe adapted for his English play.

question: Late in the twenty-four years of his bargain with Mephistopheles, Doctor Faustus demanded the most beautiful woman who had ever lived for his bedmate. Mephistopheles conjured up the spirit of the legendary Greek queen whose abduction had started the Trojan War. Faust embraced her and spoke a famous line in Christopher Marlowe's 1604 play. What is the Marlowe line that opens the scene?
answer: Was this the face that launch'd a thousand ships?
choices: Was this the face that launch'd a thousand ships?
What woman is this whose beauty doth bind?
O Helen, fair daughter of doomed Troy, return!
Now art thou come, sweet bride from far Mycenae
context: Marlowe's full couplet is one of the most famous in English literature: *Was this the face that launch'd a thousand ships / And burnt the topless towers of Ilium?* Helen, in Greek myth, was the queen of Sparta whose abduction by Paris of Troy began the ten-year siege immortalized in Homer's *Iliad*. The 'topless towers of Ilium' are the high walls of Troy.

question: During his twenty-four years bound to Mephistopheles, Doctor Faustus traveled across Europe working invisible magic and tricks. He visited Rome and mocked Pope Adrian VI by snatching food from his table at a feast. He visited the imperial court of Holy Roman Emperor Charles V and conjured up famous historical figures from the past. Which figure did Charles V most want to see conjured?
answer: Alexander the Great and his Persian queen Roxana
choices: Alexander the Great and his Persian queen Roxana
Cicero giving a speech in the Roman Senate
Achilles at the gates of Troy in full armor
King David of Israel playing his harp before Saul
context: In Marlowe's *Doctor Faustus*, the conjuring of Alexander the Great in the court of Charles V is one of the central spectacular scenes. Charles V (1500–1558) was the most powerful European ruler of the early 16th century — King of Spain, Holy Roman Emperor, ruler of the Spanish American empire. The real Charles V was a deeply religious Catholic, which made the visit of an explicit devil-conjurer a dramatic provocation in Marlowe's play.

question: After his arrest for the threat against Gessler with his second arrow, William Tell was put on a boat to be taken across Lake Lucerne to a Habsburg dungeon. A violent storm rose on the lake. Tell was the strongest oarsman aboard; the soldiers unchained his hands so he could row. As the boat approached a great flat rock projecting from the cliff, Tell drove the boat against the rock and leaped onto it — then kicked the boat back out into the storm. He then made his way alone across the mountains to the road leading to Gessler's castle at Kussnacht. What did Tell do there?
answer: Hid behind a tree and shot Gessler dead with his second arrow
choices: Hid behind a tree and shot Gessler dead with his second arrow
Burned the castle of Kussnacht to the ground that night
Surrendered at the castle gate and was hanged at dawn
Pleaded for mercy and asked the bailiff's forgiveness
context: The killing of Gessler by Tell in a forest gully near Kussnacht is the central revolutionary moment of the William Tell legend — the spark of Swiss independence from Habsburg rule. Friedrich Schiller's *Wilhelm Tell* (1804) dramatizes the scene. The flat rock where Tell jumped from the boat — *Tellsplatte* — is still a tourist site on Lake Lucerne.

question: In the same legendary period of the William Tell story, three men met by torchlight on a meadow called the Rütli above Lake Lucerne — one each from the Swiss cantons of Uri, Schwyz, and Unterwalden — and swore a sacred oath to defend each other against Habsburg oppression. The William Tell story is often linked to this oath; Tell himself is sometimes said to have been present. The three men swore to be of one heart against the foreign tyrant. What is this oath called in Swiss tradition?
answer: The Rütli Oath of 1291
choices: The Rütli Oath of 1291
The Lucerne Compact of 1308
The Altdorf Pact of 1273
The Schaffhausen Bond of 1315
context: The Federal Charter of 1291, sometimes called the Rütli Oath, is the traditional founding document of the Swiss Confederation. The original parchment is preserved at Schwyz. Whether the meeting on the Rütli meadow happened exactly as legend describes is unknown, but the alliance of the three Forest Cantons against the Habsburgs is a well-documented historical fact. August 1 — the traditional Rütli Oath date — is the Swiss national holiday.

question: El Cid (the Castilian knight Rodrigo Díaz de Vivar) had taken the great city of Valencia from the Almoravid Muslims in 1094 AD and ruled it as his own kingdom. He died there in 1099 AD. The Almoravids besieged the city again, hoping the loss of El Cid would break Christian morale. According to legend, El Cid's widow Doña Jimena and her counselors had a strange idea. What did they do with El Cid's body?
answer: Embalmed it, dressed it in armor, and strapped it to his horse Babieca
choices: Embalmed it, dressed it in armor, and strapped it to his horse Babieca
Burned it on a great pyre visible from the besieging army
Sealed it in the great altar of Valencia's cathedral
Carried it ahead of the army in a glass coffin
context: El Cid's embalmed body, propped upright in the saddle of his beloved white warhorse Babieca, led one final charge out of the gates of Valencia at dawn. The besieging Almoravid army, seeing the dead Cid riding in front of his Castilian cavalry, broke and fled in terror. The story is told in the *Cantar de Mio Cid* (c. 1200), the oldest surviving epic poem in Castilian Spanish.

question: On Saint John's Day (June 26, 1284 AD), the Pied Piper returned to the town of Hamelin in Lower Saxony — the town that had refused to pay him after he had piped all the rats into the River Weser to drown. He played a new and different tune on his pipe. One hundred and thirty children of the town followed him. He led them away — and not one was ever seen again. According to the Hamelin chronicles, where did the piper lead the children?
answer: Into a hole in a mountain called the Koppen, which closed behind them
choices: Into a hole in a mountain called the Koppen, which closed behind them
Out to sea on a ship that sailed beyond the western horizon
Into a cave under the River Weser that flooded shut behind them
Onto a winding road south that no one ever traveled again
context: The Hamelin chronicles record the date June 26, 1284 — one of the most specific medieval-legendary dates in European tradition. Hamelin still has a street called Bungelosenstrasse — 'Drumless Street' — where no music or dancing is allowed in memory of the lost children. The Brothers Grimm collected the story in their *German Legends* (1816). A possible historical kernel may be a 13th-century children's migration into eastern Europe.

question: After Sir Mordred had usurped the throne of Britain while his uncle King Arthur was campaigning in France, Arthur raced home with his weary army. The two hosts met at last on Salisbury Plain at the Battle of Camlann. Arthur's army was the broken remnant of the Round Table; Mordred's was a mixture of British rebels and Saxon mercenaries. A truce was being negotiated between the two camps under careful conditions — both sides agreed to send heralds bearing white wands; neither army was to draw a sword unless an enemy first drew one. The two kings approached each other on horseback to seal the truce. At that moment, a soldier in one of the rear ranks felt a small movement near his boot. He looked down and saw a snake about to strike at him. He drew his sword on instinct to kill it. What did the watching armies see?
answer: A drawn sword — both armies attacked at once and the slaughter began
choices: A drawn sword — both armies attacked at once and the slaughter began
A flash of light — the heralds shouted treachery and fled
A signal arrow — the dragon banner of Wessex broke ranks
A king's hand raised — the trumpets sounded retreat too late
context: Both armies wiped each other out at Camlann. The battle is the central tragedy of Malory's *Le Morte d'Arthur* — a tiny accident undoing kingdoms. By evening only Arthur, Sir Bedivere, and the dying Sir Lucan remained on Arthur's side. Mordred had fallen on Arthur's spear; Arthur fell on Mordred's sword as Mordred drove it home with his last strength.

question: Sir Mordred, the traitor king who had seized the throne of Britain while King Arthur campaigned in France against Sir Lancelot, faced his uncle on Salisbury Plain at the catastrophic Battle of Camlann. By evening the field was carpeted with the dead of both armies, and only a few men still stood on either side. Arthur saw Mordred standing apart leaning on his sword. He took a heavy spear from Sir Lucan and rushed at him crying 'Traitor, now is thy death-day come!' Mordred rushed forward to meet him. Arthur ran the spear through Mordred's body up to the haft. What did Mordred do with his last strength as he died on the spear?
answer: Pushed himself further up the shaft and split Arthur's helmet with his sword
choices: Pushed himself further up the shaft and split Arthur's helmet with his sword
Bit his uncle on the throat as they fell together
Called the name of Morgause his mother and died screaming
Drove a dagger through Arthur's chain mail at his ribs
context: Mordred forced himself up the spear shaft to reach his uncle. He died as he struck — and the blow cut through Arthur's helmet into the skull. Arthur fell. The three loyal men remaining — Sir Bedivere, Sir Lucan, and Sir Lucan's brother — carried him from the field. Lucan died of his own wounds lifting Arthur to his feet. Only Bedivere was left to throw Excalibur back into the lake and witness the three queens taking Arthur to Avalon.

question: After the catastrophe of Camlann, the mortally-wounded King Arthur was carried by Sir Bedivere to a small chapel near a misty lake. Arthur ordered Bedivere to take the sword Excalibur and throw it back into the lake, for the sword had come from the lake and must return there before Arthur could die in peace. Bedivere went to the water's edge and looked at the golden hilt and the jeweled pommel, and could not bear to throw away such a sword. He hid it under a tree and came back to Arthur saying he had thrown it. Arthur, weak and bleeding, said only: 'What did you see?' Bedivere said: 'I saw nothing but the waves and the wind.' Arthur called him a liar and told him to go again. The second time, Bedivere hid the sword and lied a second time. Arthur this time threatened him with his own death if he disobeyed a third time. What did Bedivere finally see when he obeyed?
answer: An arm in white samite caught the sword and brandished it three times
choices: An arm in white samite caught the sword and brandished it three times
A great white swan flew down and bore the blade across the water
A black-robed ferryman rowed out and took the sword from his hand
A flame leaped from the lake and consumed the sword to bright ash
context: Bedivere returned to Arthur weeping. The dying king said simply: 'Now I know thou art a true knight at last.' Then Arthur asked to be carried to the water. A black-draped barge slipped from the mist, rowed by three queens — Morgan le Fay, the Queen of Northgalis, and the Queen of the Waste Lands. They lifted Arthur on board and the barge disappeared. Bedivere was left alone on the bank. Malory's ending is one of the great closing scenes in English literature.

question: On the misty shore where Sir Bedivere had just finished throwing Excalibur back to the Lady of the Lake, a black-draped barge slipped silently from the fog. Three queens stood on its deck weeping. Bedivere, frightened, asked Arthur who they were. Arthur named them: Morgan le Fay his half-sister, the Queen of Northgalis, and the Queen of the Waste Lands. They lifted the wounded king from the rocks onto the boat. As the barge began to pull away, Bedivere fell on his knees and begged: 'My lord Arthur, what shall become of me now ye go from me, and leave me here alone among mine enemies?' What was Arthur's answer to him?
answer: Comfort thyself, and do as well as thou mayst, for in me is no trust to trust in
choices: Comfort thyself, and do as well as thou mayst, for in me is no trust to trust in
Pray ever for my soul wherever thy own poor steps shall fall
Take Excalibur from the water and rule Britain in my own stead
Seek out my son Mordred's son and finish what we two began
context: Arthur told Bedivere he was going to the vale of Avilion (Avalon) to heal his grievous wound, and that Bedivere should never see him again, though some men say King Arthur shall come again. The barge vanished into the mist. Sir Bedivere lived out his remaining years as a hermit in a chapel near where the boat had departed, praying for Arthur's soul. The line *Rex quondam, rexque futurus* — 'the once and future king' — was carved on Arthur's reputed tomb at Glastonbury Abbey.

question: Of the four knights who had pressed deepest into the Quest of the Holy Grail — Sir Galahad, Sir Percival, Sir Bors, and Sir Lancelot — the first three arrived together at last in the eastern city of Sarras after a long sea voyage in a holy ship. There a vision of the apostle Joseph of Arimathea appeared and celebrated a mass at the holy table. Galahad alone among the three was permitted to look directly into the Grail itself. The other two knelt at a respectful distance and saw only its outer brightness. After Galahad's vision he turned to Percival and Bors and asked Percival to send a message to his father Sir Lancelot. What did he say to take to Lancelot?
answer: Salute me to my lord Sir Lancelot my father, and bid him remember of this unstable world
choices: Salute me to my lord Sir Lancelot my father, and bid him remember of this unstable world
Tell my lord father to seek not the Grail himself, lest he too die in joy
Carry to him this crystal vial of holy oil for his old wounds
Bring my white shield and broken spear to him at Camelot
context: After speaking the message Galahad knelt before the altar and prayed. His soul rose visibly from his body and was borne up by a host of angels. Galahad's death is the perfect saintly ending in Malory's *Le Morte d'Arthur*. Percival became a hermit at Sarras and died within a year of grief. Only Bors returned to Camelot to tell Arthur the story. The Grail was carried up to heaven with Galahad and has never been seen on earth since.

question: After King Arthur died at Camlann and Queen Guinevere took the veil at Amesbury Abbey, Sir Lancelot crossed back from France to find the kingdom ruined. He visited Guinevere once at the convent; she refused to embrace him and asked him to leave her forever and pray for her soul. Lancelot rode then to Glastonbury, where an old hermit who had been the Archbishop of Canterbury lived with one priest. He knocked at the gate and asked to take the brown habit of the hermits. When Guinevere died seven years later, the hermit-Lancelot dreamed of her death three nights in a row and rose to walk to Amesbury to collect her body. With whom did Lancelot make the seven-day funeral procession from Amesbury to Glastonbury Abbey?
answer: Seven other former Round Table knights who had become hermits with him
choices: Seven other former Round Table knights who had become hermits with him
Twelve nuns of Amesbury who had attended Guinevere in her death
King Mark of Cornwall and the surviving Cornish barons
Three young squires from his castle Joyous Gard in France
context: The seven hermits were Sir Bors, Sir Ector de Maris, Sir Blamore, Sir Bleoberis, Sir Villiers, Sir Clarrus, and Sir Gahalantine. They walked the body from Amesbury all the way to Glastonbury Abbey, where Lancelot laid Guinevere in the grave beside Arthur. Lancelot would not eat or drink for six weeks afterward and died of grief. Malory's *Le Morte d'Arthur* (1485) ends with the seven hermit-knights placing Lancelot beside Guinevere and Arthur — the Round Table at last laid to rest at Glastonbury.

question: The wizard Merlin — born of a holy princess in a convent through a demonic illusion, then baptized into Christian holiness — was the architect of King Arthur's rise. He arranged Arthur's secret birth by enchanting King Uther Pendragon into the form of Duke Gorlois, fostered the child with Sir Ector, placed the sword in the stone in the London churchyard, and crowned Arthur at fifteen. He took Arthur to the Lady of the Lake to receive Excalibur. He warned Arthur of the doom that Mordred would bring. He prophesied his own death at the hand of the enchantress he loved — and walked into it anyway. According to Malory's *Le Morte d'Arthur*, how did Merlin meet his end?
answer: Imprisoned by Nimue under a great stone using his own enchantments
choices: Imprisoned by Nimue under a great stone using his own enchantments
Slain by his own apprentice in a sword duel at Avalon
Burned at the stake by Saxon raiders at Tintagel Castle
Drowned beneath the lake when the Lady refused his suit
context: Nimue (also called Vivienne) — the young enchantress Merlin loved — learned all his secret arts from him and then used them to seal him under the stone. Merlin foresaw exactly how he would die; the prophetic knowledge could not save him from the love that drove him into the trap. Without Merlin's counsel the Round Table would slowly unravel — Mordred's rise, the discovery of the affair, the civil war, and finally Camlann would all unfold while the wizard who could have prevented them lay imprisoned beneath the stone.

question: In Chrétien de Troyes' *Perceval, the Story of the Grail* (c. 1180), the young Sir Percival arrived as a guest one evening at a mysterious river castle whose lord lay wounded on a couch beside the great hall fire. The wound — said to be in the thigh — would never heal, and his country had become a wasteland. As the lord and the boy talked, a strange procession passed through the hall: a young man bearing a spear from whose tip a single drop of blood ran down to his hand, and then a maiden carrying a great covered chalice from which a holy light shone. Percival had been trained by his mother and his tutor never to question his elders too freely. So he stayed silent and watched the procession pass. The next morning the castle was empty and abandoned. What was the question Percival should have asked that night?
answer: Whom does the Holy Grail serve in this castle?
choices: Whom does the Holy Grail serve in this castle?
Who pierced this holy lance with so much blood?
How came thy wound that will not heal, my lord?
What land is this that lies so dark around us?
context: Had Percival asked, both the king and the wasteland would have been healed at once. His silence cost him many years of wandering before he returned to ask the question. The wounded king was called the Fisher King; the lance was identified in later tradition with the lance of Longinus that pierced Christ's side at the crucifixion; the Grail was the cup of the Last Supper. Chrétien left his poem unfinished at his death — the Grail mystery has tantalized European literature ever since.

question: The British king Vortigern — who had invited the Saxons Hengist and Horsa into Britain as mercenaries — was hated by his own people and forced to retreat into the mountains of Snowdonia in Wales. He tried to build a great refuge-tower there, but each night the walls his masons built by day fell down. His sorcerers told him the foundations needed to be wetted with the blood of a fatherless boy. The boy his soldiers brought him was the young Merlin, conceived without a mortal father. Merlin laughed at the sorcerers and said the real problem was something else beneath the foundations. What did Merlin reveal when the workmen dug into the ground?
answer: Two dragons sleeping in an underground pool, one red and one white
choices: Two dragons sleeping in an underground pool, one red and one white
A buried Roman emperor's tomb full of golden treasure
A great river of fire flowing under the mountain's roots
The bones of a giant chained beneath the rock for blasphemy
context: The dragons woke and fought. The white dragon (the Saxons) seemed to be winning at first, but in the end the red dragon (the Britons) would conquer. Merlin's prophecy at Vortigern's tower is the founding moment of his fame and one of the most famous scenes in Geoffrey of Monmouth's *History of the Kings of Britain* (c. 1136). The red dragon of the prophecy is still the symbol on the modern flag of Wales — *Y Ddraig Goch*.

question: Sir Gawain, riding through deep winter snow to keep his appointment at the Green Chapel a year and a day after the beheading game at Camelot, was sheltered for three nights at a fine castle in the wilderness. The castle's lord went hunting each of the three days; the lord's wife stayed home and tested Gawain with seductive offers in her husband's absence. They agreed to exchange whatever each won that day at evening. Gawain gave the lord all the kisses the lady had given him each day. But on the third day the lady gave Gawain something he did not give to her host — something she swore would protect him from death at the Green Knight's axe. What was it?
answer: A green silk girdle that would shield the wearer from any wound
choices: A green silk girdle that would shield the wearer from any wound
A gold ring engraved with the secret name of God
A silver pendant containing a relic of Saint Christopher
A black raven's feather to be worn in his helmet's crest
context: Gawain kept the green girdle hidden from his host. At the Green Chapel, the Green Knight swung the axe three times — pulling back the first two strokes — and on the third merely nicked Gawain's neck. Then the Green Knight revealed he had been Bertilak, the castle's lord, in enchanted shape. The girdle's owner was the host who had tested him. Gawain wore the green sash thereafter as a mark of his shame; the whole Round Table adopted green sashes in his honor. The 14th-century poem *Sir Gawain and the Green Knight* is one of the great works of Middle English.

question: In the summer of 778 AD, Charlemagne had spent seven years campaigning against the Saracens in Spain. The Saracen king Marsile of Saragossa, fearing total defeat, sent ambassadors offering false peace. Charlemagne sent the paladin Ganelon — Roland's stepfather — to negotiate. Roland had insulted Ganelon by suggesting his name for the dangerous mission. Ganelon, burning with hatred, accepted Marsile's gold and betrayed Roland. He told Marsile that Roland would command the rear-guard through the narrow pass of Roncevaux. The Saracens prepared an ambush of a hundred thousand men against Roland's rear-guard of twenty thousand. As the ambush began, Roland's loyal friend Oliver climbed a hill, saw the huge enemy host, and three times begged Roland to blow the ivory war-horn Olifant to summon Charlemagne back. What was Roland's reason for refusing all three times?
answer: It would be a shame and a disgrace to his family and to fair France
choices: It would be a shame and a disgrace to his family and to fair France
Charlemagne is too far across the mountains to come in time
Olifant has been damaged in battle and cannot now be blown
He has already sworn an oath never to blow it without leave
context: Roland refused for hours — too proud to admit the rear-guard could be overwhelmed — until almost every paladin was dead. Then he finally blew Olifant three times; the third blast burst the veins in his temples. Charlemagne arrived too late to save the rear-guard but pursued the Saracens all the way back to Saragossa and burned it. Ganelon was torn apart by four horses at the trial in Aachen. *The Song of Roland* (c. 1100) is the earliest major work of French literature, the founding epic of paladin-romance.

question: As the slaughter at Roncevaux Pass continued through the afternoon of 778 AD, the twelve paladins of Charlemagne's rear-guard fell one by one. Roland's loyal friend Oliver was struck a blow on the back of the head from behind by the Saracen Marganice and fought on with darkened sight, his blood running into his eyes — half-blind, he gave Roland himself a stunning blow without recognizing him. Roland called Oliver by name. Oliver wept and asked Roland's pardon, then died in his friend's arms. Archbishop Turpin of Reims, the paladin who was also a churchman, was wounded again and again in the breast but kept fighting and giving absolution to the dying knights. Of all the paladins of Charlemagne's twelve, who was the last alive beside Roland to die?
answer: Archbishop Turpin of Reims
choices: Archbishop Turpin of Reims
Ogier the Dane
Renaud de Montauban
Naimes of Bavaria
context: Archbishop Turpin gave absolution to Roland and the dying paladins, then succumbed to his wounds with prayer on his lips. Roland alone stood at the end. He set Olifant to his lips and finally blew the great horn — three times, the third blast killing him. Charlemagne heard the sound across thirty miles. He arrived at the pass at sunset and found Roland on a green hill lying on his back facing south toward Spain, with Olifant and Durendal beneath his body. The poet of *The Song of Roland* (c. 1100) gives each paladin a long death scene; Turpin's is one of the most moving.

question: On the night before the rear-guard at Roncevaux was ambushed, Charlemagne — sleeping in his tent far away across the Pyrenees in France — had a strange dream. He saw a beautiful eagle being attacked by a leopard. Then he saw a stronger lion strike a great blow against the leopard. He woke knowing it was a warning he could not understand. In the medieval reading of *The Song of Roland* (c. 1100), the eagle stood for Roland. What did the leopard and the lion stand for?
answer: The leopard for Ganelon's treachery; the lion for the eventual vengeance
choices: The leopard for Ganelon's treachery; the lion for the eventual vengeance
The leopard for Marsile of Spain; the lion for Charlemagne himself
The leopard for Roland's pride; the lion for God's judgment
The leopard for the Saracens at Saragossa; the lion for the Pope
context: Charlemagne had several prophetic dreams during the campaign — the medieval poet uses them to deepen the sense of fate. After Roland's death, Charlemagne pursued the Saracens all the way to Saragossa, captured the city, killed Marsile, baptized Marsile's queen Bramimonde, and returned to Aachen for the trial and execution of Ganelon. The dream-figures map onto exactly that vengeance arc. *The Song of Roland* survives in the Oxford Manuscript copied around 1130 AD.

question: Roland, mortally wounded after blowing his great war-horn Olifant three times — the third blast bursting the veins of his temples — climbed alone to the top of a green hill at Roncevaux Pass. His twelve paladins were all dead around him. Charlemagne and the main army were still racing back through the mountains and would not arrive in time to see him alive. Roland tried three times to break his sword Durendal against a great marble rock, to keep it from Saracen hands. The blade did not break — only the rock split in two. Roland then lay down and placed Olifant and Durendal beneath his body to hide them. What was the direction his face was turned as he died?
answer: Toward Spain, so he would die facing the enemy unrepentant
choices: Toward Spain, so he would die facing the enemy unrepentant
Toward Aachen, so his soul could fly straight to the emperor
Toward Rome and the Pope, so the saints might pray for him
Down at the earth in shame for the destruction of the rear-guard
context: Charlemagne arrived at sunset and found Roland on the hill, face turned south toward Spain — refusing to die looking back at his own kingdom. The emperor wept and tore his beard. The poet of *The Song of Roland* (c. 1100) describes the moment in unforgettable detail. Roland was buried at Charlemagne's chapel in Aachen; the body of his friend Oliver was buried beside him. The bones of the rear-guard were buried in a long mass grave at the pass.

question: Beowulf had ruled the Geats of southern Sweden as a wise and peaceful king for fifty winters when a slave hiding in an old burial mound stole one cup from an enormous treasure hoard. The dragon that had brooded over the gold for three hundred years woke in fury. It came out at night and burned Geatish farms and villages — even Beowulf's own great hall. The old king, now grey and stiff with age, knew that his time had come. He took up his great iron shield, his chain mail, and the sword Naegling that had served him long. With twelve picked companions he rode to the dragon's barrow. He sent his men back and went forward alone, calling the dragon out. The dragon's first fire-blast scorched Beowulf's iron shield. The sword Naegling broke in his hand at the dragon's hide. Eleven of his twelve companions fled the fire. Who alone stood by him?
answer: His young kinsman Wiglaf, who would inherit the kingdom
choices: His young kinsman Wiglaf, who would inherit the kingdom
His old steward Hygd, who tended his hall
Unferth, returning the borrowed sword Hrunting
The slave who had stolen the cup, now bound in repentance
context: Wiglaf — a young warrior of the Waegmunding clan, the same clan as Beowulf — was the only one of the twelve picked companions who stayed. Together they killed the dragon: Beowulf with his great knife to the belly, Wiglaf striking the throat. But the dragon's fangs bit into Beowulf's neck and the venom worked into his blood. He died as the dragon died. The eleven cowards came back from the woods in shame; Wiglaf cursed them and predicted their families would soon lose their lands forever.

question: Beowulf died of the dragon's venom shortly after the killing of the dragon in his fiftieth year of rule. Before he died, he asked his young kinsman Wiglaf — the only companion who had stood with him in the fight — to fetch some of the dragon's hoard so he might see it before his eyes failed. Wiglaf carried out armfuls of cups and goblets and golden plate, but the old king was already too dim of sight to look at them clearly. Beowulf instructed Wiglaf about the burial: his ashes were to be laid in a great mound on the headland called Hronesness — Whale-Headland — high above the sea so that sailors crossing from far away would see his grave as they came in to harbor. The mound was built up in ten days. What else was placed in the mound with Beowulf's ashes?
answer: The dragon's entire treasure-hoard, cursed and useless to men
choices: The dragon's entire treasure-hoard, cursed and useless to men
The skulls of his greatest enemies in life
Only his sword Naegling and his iron-bound shield
A roll of runes recording all his deeds for posterity
context: The dragon's treasure was buried with Beowulf because the cowardly companions who had fled the fire were too ashamed to claim any of it, and Wiglaf cursed any survivor who would touch the hoard. Twelve picked warriors rode around the burning pyre singing his praises and weeping. The poem *Beowulf* survives in a single Old English manuscript from around 1000 AD — its last lines describe Beowulf as the gentlest, kindest, and most eager for fame of all kings. The poem is the oldest substantial work of English literature.

question: The treasure-hoard that the dragon had guarded for three centuries before Beowulf came to it had originally been buried in the great mound by the last survivor of a forgotten people. That last survivor had spoken a long lament over the gold — for his kinsmen were all dead and there was no one left to wear the war-helmet, to carry the polished cup, to wield the sword. The lament ended with a curse. What did Wiglaf's curse on the surviving cowards of Beowulf's twelve companions say about the gold?
answer: It would lie in the mound forever and no man would wear it
choices: It would lie in the mound forever and no man would wear it
It would bring fire to any house that took even a single piece
It would multiply each generation if buried with a king's bones
It would speak the names of its old owners on every full moon
context: Wiglaf condemned the eleven cowards to lose their lands and homes — the Geats, hearing of Beowulf's death, would soon be overrun by their enemies the Swedes. The dragon's gold was the symbolic price of that ruin. The lament of the last survivor and the curse together form one of the most haunting passages in *Beowulf* — a meditation on the futility of treasure when there is no one left to inherit it. The Sutton Hoo ship-burial in Suffolk (c. 625 AD) gives a real archaeological glimpse of the kind of treasure described.

question: The poem *Beowulf* — written in Old English alliterative verse and surviving in a single manuscript from around 1000 AD — ends with a final description of the dead king. Twelve picked warriors rode around the burning pyre on Hronesness, singing his praises in long alliterative lines, weeping for the loss of him, and predicting the disaster soon to come upon the Geats now that he was gone. The last lines of the poem are a famous four-fold epitaph for Beowulf. Which of the following best matches the four traits the poem names him for?
answer: Gentlest of men, most gracious, kindest to his people, most eager for fame
choices: Gentlest of men, most gracious, kindest to his people, most eager for fame
Strongest of warriors, fiercest of hunters, hardest of stone, bravest of all
Wisest of kings, cleverest of judges, deepest of poets, sternest of judges
Tallest of men, broadest of shoulders, swiftest of foot, sharpest of eye
context: In Old English: *manna mildust ond monðwærust, leodum liðost ond lofgeornost*. The four attributes — mild, gracious, kind, eager for fame — were the highest praise a Germanic hero could receive: a balance of courage and gentleness almost unique in the heroic literature of the period. Compare to the more bloody Norse sagas. *Beowulf* survives in a single manuscript — Cotton Vitellius A.xv — in the British Library, damaged by a fire in 1731 but still readable around the singed edges.

question: Doctor Faustus's twenty-four years of bargained pleasure on earth were almost finished. The contract he had signed in his own blood would soon come due. He sat alone in his study in Wittenberg with a great hourglass and a clock striking the quarters. Some of his old students came to ask why he looked so wretched. He told them everything — the pentagram, the demon Mephistopheles, the contract signed in blood, the twenty-four years of trivial magic, the dazzling vanity of every pleasure. He asked them to pray for him through the night but to lock their own doors against the demons. The clock struck eleven. Faust began the most famous despairing soliloquy in English drama, begging time itself to stop — for he had only one more hour. As midnight struck and the demons appeared, what was Faust's final desperate cry?
answer: I'll burn my books! Ah, Mephistopheles!
choices: I'll burn my books! Ah, Mephistopheles!
Christ, my own Savior, save me now!
Mephistopheles, hold them another hour!
Helen, my Helen, come back to me, my love!
context: Marlowe's *Doctor Faustus* (1604) ends with the demons dragging Faust off-stage shrieking. The students return at dawn to find his torn-apart body scattered across the study. The final chorus is one of the most somber in Marlowe: *Cut is the branch that might have grown full straight, / And burned is Apollo's laurel-bough, / That sometime grew within this learned man.* Goethe's two-part *Faust* (1808 and 1832) reversed Marlowe's ending — in Goethe, Faust is ultimately saved by God's grace despite the bargain.

question: Doctor Faustus, a learned scholar at the University of Wittenberg in Germany — the same university where Martin Luther would later nail his ninety-five theses — had mastered law, medicine, philosophy, and theology by his middle years. None of it satisfied him. He turned to forbidden books and conjured up the demon Mephistopheles by drawing a magical pentagram on his study floor. They struck a famous bargain. Mephistopheles would serve Faust on earth for twenty-four years, granting any knowledge or pleasure Faust desired. In exchange, Faust signed away his soul in his own blood. During the twenty-four years Mephistopheles took Faust around Europe — they visited Rome to mock the Pope, the imperial court of Charles V to conjure up Alexander the Great, and the dukedom of Vanholt to make grapes appear out of season. Of all the figures Mephistopheles conjured up for Faust, who was the bedmate?
answer: Helen of Troy, the most beautiful woman in Greek myth
choices: Helen of Troy, the most beautiful woman in Greek myth
Cleopatra of Egypt, queen and lover of Caesar
Lucretia of Rome, the model of virtue
Eve of the Garden of Eden, the first mother
context: Faust's line on seeing the conjured spirit of Helen is one of the most quoted in English drama: *Was this the face that launch'd a thousand ships, and burnt the topless towers of Ilium?* The Helen-spirit was actually a demon in Helen's shape — Mephistopheles never let Faust touch any real human soul. Marlowe's *Doctor Faustus* (1604) ends with Faust dragged off-stage at midnight as the clock strikes; Goethe's two-part *Faust* (1808 and 1832) is the great German Romantic rewrite, in which Faust is ultimately saved by God's grace.

question: The legend of Doctor Faustus had a real historical seed. There was a wandering German alchemist named Johann Georg Faust who lived in the early 16th century, claimed to be able to summon demons, and was kicked out of multiple cities for fraud and immorality. He died around 1541, supposedly when one of his alchemical experiments exploded in a Württemberg tavern — locals at the time said the devil had finally come for him. Within fifty years of his death, his story had grown into a moral folktale published as a German chapbook in 1587. What was the chapbook called that first set down the full Faust legend?
answer: The Historia von D. Johann Fausten
choices: The Historia von D. Johann Fausten
The Wittenberg Necromancer's Confession
The Conjuror's Book of Hours
The Devil's Compact and Twenty-Four Years
context: The 1587 *Historia* was the source Christopher Marlowe used for his *Tragical History of Doctor Faustus* (1604). Marlowe's English play in turn was the source for Goethe's two-part *Faust* (1808 and 1832). The phrase 'Faustian bargain' for trading long-term happiness for short-term gain comes directly from this story tradition. Goethe's version reverses the chapbook ending — Faust is ultimately saved by God's grace despite the bargain, on the theory that whoever strives constantly upward, however imperfectly, will be saved.

question: William Tell is the founding hero of Swiss independence — the marksman of the canton of Uri who refused to bow to the Habsburg bailiff Gessler's hat on the pole at Altdorf, shot an apple off his own son's head as punishment, threatened Gessler with a second arrow, escaped on a stormy lake voyage, and finally killed Gessler with that very arrow in a forest ambush near Kussnacht. According to the Swiss tradition Tell was alive during the Rütli Oath of 1291 — the secret meeting of representatives from three forest cantons on the meadow above Lake Lucerne, where they swore alliance against the Habsburgs. According to Friedrich Schiller's 1804 play *Wilhelm Tell*, what was Tell's role in the Confederation's actual founding?
answer: Symbol and inspiration, but not himself an Oath-signer
choices: Symbol and inspiration, but not himself an Oath-signer
Chief negotiator and the first man to read the oath aloud
Captain of the army that drove out the Habsburg garrisons
First president of the new Confederation at Schwyz
context: Schiller's *Wilhelm Tell* shows Tell as a private hunter who acts on his own, not as a political leader — his killing of Gessler galvanizes the Confederation but he himself does not sign the Rütli Oath. The three signers in tradition are Werner Stauffacher of Schwyz, Walter Fürst of Uri, and Arnold von Melchtal of Unterwalden. The Federal Charter of August 1, 1291 — sometimes called the Rütli Oath — survives in original parchment at the Federal Charter Museum in Schwyz. August 1 is the Swiss national holiday.

question: After William Tell was arrested for his second-arrow threat against the Habsburg bailiff Gessler, soldiers put him in chains on a boat to row him across Lake Lucerne to a Habsburg dungeon. As they crossed the lake, a violent storm rose — winds in the narrow valleys whipped the water to whitecaps. Tell, alone among the men aboard, was strong enough as an oarsman to keep the boat from foundering. Gessler ordered Tell's chains struck off so he could take the helm. As they approached a great flat rock projecting from the cliff base, Tell drove the boat against the rock and leaped onto it — then kicked the boat back out into the storm with all his strength. What did Tell then do?
answer: Climbed the cliff and ran across the mountains to ambush Gessler at Kussnacht
choices: Climbed the cliff and ran across the mountains to ambush Gessler at Kussnacht
Hid on the rock until nightfall and then swam to the far shore
Surrendered when Gessler's boat returned with backup soldiers
Threw himself back into the storm to escape pursuit by drowning
context: Tell crossed the mountains alone in the storm to lie in wait for Gessler on the road to Kussnacht Castle. He shot Gessler dead with that very same second arrow. The killing of Gessler became the revolutionary spark of the Swiss independence movement. The flat rock — *Tellsplatte* — is still a tourist site on the Lake Lucerne shore today, with a small 16th-century chapel built above it to commemorate the leap.

question: In the William Tell legend's full Swiss-Confederation context, three men met by torchlight on a meadow called the Rütli above Lake Lucerne on the night of November 7, 1307 (in Schiller's dating; the parchment Federal Charter is dated 1291). One came from each of the three Forest Cantons. They swore a sacred oath to be of one heart against the Habsburg tyrants — to defend each other in life and to remain free. According to Friedrich Schiller's 1804 play *Wilhelm Tell*, who were the three?
answer: Stauffacher of Schwyz, Fürst of Uri, and Melchtal of Unterwalden

context: The three Forest Cantons of Schwyz, Uri, and Unterwalden are the founding cantons of the Swiss Confederation. The country's name 'Switzerland' (and the Swiss themselves) come from Schwyz, the canton in the middle of the three. August 1 — the date on the parchment — is the Swiss national holiday.

question: The Castilian knight Rodrigo Díaz de Vivar — called El Cid by his Muslim allies, from the Arabic *al-sayyid* meaning 'lord' — fought as a hired soldier for both Christian and Muslim kings in the chaotic 11th-century Spain of the Reconquista. He was twice exiled by King Alfonso VI of Castile for political offenses. In 1094 AD he conquered the great Muslim city of Valencia on the Mediterranean coast and held it as his own private kingdom. He died there of natural causes in 1099 AD, at the age of about sixty. The name of El Cid's beloved white warhorse — gifted to him as a foal by his godfather, the priest who had advised him to choose the worst-looking colt in the herd — has become almost as famous as his own. What was the horse called?
answer: Babieca
choices: Babieca
Bayard
Tizona
Colada
context: The horse's name *Babieca* means 'stupid one' or 'idiot' in old Castilian — supposedly because the young Rodrigo had picked the homeliest colt in the corral as a test of his judgment. Babieca proved to be the finest warhorse in Spain. El Cid's two great swords were Colada and Tizona; Tizona is still on display at the Burgos Cathedral. Babieca outlived his master by two and a half years and was buried at the monastery of San Pedro de Cardeña.

question: After El Cid (Rodrigo Díaz de Vivar) died of natural causes at Valencia in 1099 AD, the Almoravid Muslims besieged the city again — hoping the loss of the great Christian captain would break Castilian morale. According to the *Cantar de Mio Cid* (c. 1200), the widow Doña Jimena and her counselors had a strange idea to keep the spirit of the Cid alive in battle. They embalmed his body, dressed it in his armor, propped it upright in the saddle of his beloved warhorse Babieca, and strapped it in place with leather thongs. Then at dawn the gates of Valencia were thrown open. What did the Almoravid army see and what did they do?
answer: El Cid riding in front of his cavalry — they broke and fled in terror
choices: El Cid riding in front of his cavalry — they broke and fled in terror
Empty walls of Valencia — they stormed the city at noon
A monk on a white mule carrying El Cid's banner — they laughed
Doña Jimena alone on the road — they accepted her surrender
context: The Almoravid army, seeing the dead Cid riding in front of his cavalry as if alive, broke and fled in terror. Valencia held out for two more years before the Castilians finally evacuated and burned it rather than let it fall to the Muslims. El Cid's body and Babieca were taken back to the monastery of San Pedro de Cardeña near Burgos for burial. The *Cantar de Mio Cid* (c. 1200) is the oldest surviving epic poem in Castilian Spanish and the founding work of Spanish literature.

question: The legend of the Pied Piper of Hamelin is unusual among medieval European folk tales because it can be dated to a specific year, June 26, 1284 AD, and is recorded in the actual town chronicles of Hamelin (Hameln) in Lower Saxony. The story has two parts: first the piper drove the town's rats into the River Weser by playing a tune, and the town refused to pay him the agreed thousand guilders; then the piper returned on Saint John's Day and played a different tune that drew the children of the town instead. One hundred and thirty children followed him. They were led into a hole in a hillside called the Koppen which closed behind them. According to the Hamelin town tradition, how many children were left behind in the town?
answer: Three — a blind boy, a deaf girl, and one lame child who could not keep up
choices: Three — a blind boy, a deaf girl, and one lame child who could not keep up
None — the entire generation of Hamelin children was lost
Twelve — the very oldest who stayed to help their parents
Seven — exactly one for each surviving guild master
context: The three left-behind children — blind, deaf, and lame — appear in many versions of the story. The blind boy could not see where the piper was leading; the deaf girl could not hear the tune; the lame child could not keep up. They were the only witnesses to what had happened. Hamelin still has a Bungelosenstrasse — Drumless Street — where no music or dancing is allowed in memory of the lost children. The Pied Piper window at the Hamelin Marktkirche, dating from before 1660, is the oldest surviving visual record of the legend.

question: The legend of the Pied Piper of Hamelin (June 26, 1284 AD) is one of the few medieval German folk tales with a specific dated origin. Modern historians have proposed several explanations for the lost children of Hamelin beyond the literal supernatural one. One leading hypothesis is that the children of Hamelin actually emigrated as a group to settle new lands in eastern Europe, recruited by a *lokator* — a medieval colonization agent who wore brightly-coloured clothes to attract attention. In which direction does the historical-kernel theory suggest the children went?
answer: East — to colonize new German settlements in Pomerania, Transylvania, or Moravia
choices: East — to colonize new German settlements in Pomerania, Transylvania, or Moravia

South — across the Alps as the Children's Crusade of 1212

context: Thirteenth-century Germany was the height of the *Ostsiedlung* — the eastward migration of German peasants into Slavic lands like Pomerania, Silesia, Transylvania, and Moravia. The *lokator* was a real medieval profession: an agent in colorful clothes who recruited young settlers for the new towns. The Brothers Grimm collected the Hamelin story in their *Deutsche Sagen* (1816). Robert Browning's 1842 poem *The Pied Piper of Hamelin* fixed the story in English popular tradition.

question: Roland's death at the Pass of Roncevaux in 778 AD gave Western Europe its founding paladin legend — *The Song of Roland* (c. 1100) became the model for centuries of chivalric romance. Roland's relics were claimed by many medieval cathedrals. His ivory war-horn Olifant — carved from a single elephant tusk and reinforced with gold and jewels — was said to have been recovered from beneath his body by Charlemagne and brought back to Aachen as a holy relic. Other cathedrals claimed pieces of his sword Durendal, or his armor, or his blood-stained shield. Which cathedral has historically claimed to display the most famous Olifant?
answer: The Cathedral of Aachen in modern Germany
choices: The Cathedral of Aachen in modern Germany
Reims Cathedral in northern France
The Basilica of Saint Denis near Paris
Saragossa Cathedral in northern Spain
context: Aachen — Charlemagne's capital — was the natural home of the Olifant tradition. Roland was originally said to have been buried at Aachen with Charlemagne's own permission, but other traditions placed him at Blaye in southwestern France, Saint Romain de Blaye, or Saint Denis. The historical Olifants of Aachen and other treasuries are oliphant horns of unknown specific provenance, mostly carved in southern Italy or Byzantium in the 11th–12th centuries — they are old enough to look ancient but not old enough to be Roland's actual horn from 778.

question: Robert Browning's 1842 poem *The Pied Piper of Hamelin: A Child's Story* fixed the legend in English-speaking popular tradition. Browning gives a memorable description of the piper's clothes, the rats fleeing from cellar to river, the angry refusal of the mayor to pay, and the children dancing after the piper into the hillside. Near the end of the poem Browning describes a single boy who reached the hillside last and saw the hole closing. The boy lived to old age and would never play music again, telling visitors what he had heard inside. According to Browning's poem, what did the boy say he had heard the piper promise the children?
answer: A joyous land of fountains, fruit trees, and golden bees
choices: A joyous land of fountains, fruit trees, and golden bees
A kingdom where Christ Himself would crown them as princes
A nation across the sea where rats had no power
A field of unbroken snow that would never melt
context: Browning's 1842 poem ends with a moral aimed at the mayor and his fellow citizens: *And, whether they pipe us free, from rats or from mice, / If we've promised them aught, let us keep our promise.* Browning wrote the poem for the young son of the actor William Macready, who was bedridden and asked for something to illustrate. The Brothers Grimm had collected the original German legend in *Deutsche Sagen* (1816); Browning's English verse remains the version most read today by English-speaking children.
